uni-cse-se.title: Software Engineering (B.Tech CSE)
uni-cse-se.description: Process models and Agile, requirements, estimation and planning, design and patterns, testing, quality, maintenance and configuration management — a complete B.Tech software-engineering course with worked numericals.

courses.title: Unit 1 · Software Process Models & Agile
courses.summary: What makes software engineering different, the classic life-cycle models (waterfall, V-model, incremental, prototyping, spiral, RAD), and modern Agile practice — the Agile Manifesto, Scrum, XP, Kanban and DevOps.
outcomes: Learners can describe each SDLC model with its strengths and risks
Learners can choose a suitable model for a project scenario
Learners can explain Scrum's roles, events and artefacts
Learners can relate DevOps and CI/CD to the life cycle

scenes.text: A ticketing website crashes every festival season; each fix breaks something else.
Writing code is not enough — teams need disciplined ways to specify, design, test and evolve software.

steps.title: Software and its characteristics
steps.body:
Software = programs + documentation + data + configuration. Unlike hardware, it does not wear out but **deteriorates** due to changes (the idealised failure curve rises with each change); it is engineered, not manufactured; it is easy to change but hard to change *correctly*.
The **software crisis** (late 1960s onward): projects over budget, late, unreliable, hard to maintain → the discipline of software engineering (term popularised at the 1968 NATO conference).

steps.title: Generic process activities
steps.body: Communication → planning → modelling (analysis + design) → construction (code + test) → deployment, plus umbrella activities: project tracking, risk management, quality assurance, configuration management, reviews, measurement.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Hardware vs software failure curves
steps.body: Hardware: bathtub curve (infant mortality, steady, wear-out). Software: high early failure rate falls as bugs are fixed, then **spikes with each change** and slowly trends upward — so maintenance quality matters more than 'wear'.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Cost of late fixes
steps.body: If a defect costs ₹1 to fix in requirements, industry rules of thumb put it at roughly 10× in design/coding and far more after release. Catching ambiguity during requirements review is the cheapest quality activity (exact multipliers vary between studies).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Saying software 'wears out' like hardware.
- Equating software engineering with programming.
- Treating documentation as optional extra work.

statements.s: Software deteriorates mainly because of changes, not physical wear.
The term 'software engineering' was popularised at a 1968 NATO conference.
Software is manufactured like hardware.
Quality assurance is an umbrella activity.
Fixing defects after release is usually cheapest.

quiz.why: Software is more than code. It includes programs, documentation, data and configuration.

options: projects late, over budget and unreliable
quiz.why: The software crisis (1960s onward) was the experience of projects running late, over budget and unreliable.
Umbrella activities, such as risk management, quality assurance and configuration management, run across all phases of a project.

quiz.q: Software failure rate rises over time mainly due to
quiz.why: Software does not wear out, but its failure rate rises over time because changes introduce new defects. This is software deterioration.

quiz.q: The cheapest time to remove a requirements defect
quiz.why: A defect is cheapest to fix at the stage where it is introduced. Fixing a requirements defect during requirements avoids rework in design, code and tests.

story.title: Building a bridge vs building an app

scenes.text: A bridge needs every detail fixed before construction — a sequence of phases.
A startup app needs to show something to users quickly and change it often.

steps.title: Models
steps.body:
- **Waterfall:** requirements → design → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance, each phase completed and signed off. Good for stable, well-understood requirements; late feedback, costly change.
- **V-model:** each development phase paired with a test level (requirements ↔ acceptance testing, system design ↔ system testing, architecture ↔ integration testing, module design ↔ unit testing). Common in safety-critical work.
- **Incremental:** deliver the system in increments, each adding functionality.
- **Prototyping:** build a throwaway or evolutionary prototype to clarify requirements.
- **Spiral (Boehm):** iterations through four quadrants — objectives, **risk analysis**, development & test, planning; risk-driven.
- **RAD:** short time-boxed development with heavy reuse and user involvement.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Choose a model
steps.body:
(a) Pacemaker firmware with regulatory approval → **V-model** (traceable verification).
(b) A new kind of AI app whose users can't describe what they want → **prototyping** or Agile.
(c) A large defence system with major technical risks → **spiral**.
(d) A payroll system with fixed, well-known rules → **waterfall/incremental**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Spiral loop
steps.body: One spiral loop for a payment gateway: determine objectives (UPI + cards), identify and resolve risks (fraud, bank API limits — build a prototype), develop and test the increment, plan the next loop with customer review.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling the spiral model 'waterfall with loops' and forgetting it is **risk-driven**.
- Delivering a throwaway prototype as the product.
- Thinking the V-model has no coding phase (coding sits at the bottom of the V).

activity.prompt: Match the model to its hallmark
pairs: Each phase paired with a test level
Clarify requirements with an early model

quiz.q: Best model when requirements are unclear
quiz.why: When requirements are unclear, a prototype lets users react to something concrete. That helps discover the real needs.
Barry Boehm proposed the spiral model, a risk-driven process.

quiz.q: In the V-model, unit testing pairs with
quiz.why: In the V-model, each development phase has a matching test level. Unit testing pairs with the module (detailed) design.
In waterfall, working software appears only late, so feedback comes late and changes are costly.
A throwaway prototype is built to learn what is needed, and then discarded. The real system is then built properly.

scenes.text: A fintech team promises a usable feature every two weeks and asks users for feedback each time.
That rhythm is Scrum, one way of working in an Agile style.

steps.title: Agile Manifesto (2001)
steps.body: Four values: **individuals and interactions** over processes and tools; **working software** over comprehensive documentation; **customer collaboration** over contract negotiation; **responding to change** over following a plan (the items on the right still have value). Backed by 12 principles (frequent delivery, welcome change, sustainable pace, self-organising teams, reflection…).

steps.title: Scrum essentials (per the Scrum Guide)
steps.body:
- **Accountabilities:** Product Owner (maximises value, owns the Product Backlog), Scrum Master (helps the team use Scrum effectively), Developers.
- **Events:** the **Sprint** (fixed length, one month or less) containing Sprint Planning, **Daily Scrum** (15 minutes), Sprint Review, Sprint Retrospective.
- **Artefacts:** Product Backlog (commitment: Product Goal), Sprint Backlog (Sprint Goal), Increment (Definition of Done).
**XP** practices: pair programming, TDD, continuous integration, refactoring, small releases. **Kanban:** visualise work, limit work in progress (WIP), manage flow.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Velocity forecast
steps.body: A team completed 30, 26 and 34 story points in the last three sprints → average velocity 30. A backlog of 240 points needs about 240 / 30 = **8 sprints** (a forecast, not a promise).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Kanban WIP
steps.body: A board's 'Testing' column has a WIP limit of 3. It already holds 3 cards, so developers who finish coding should **help test** rather than start new work — the limit exposes the bottleneck.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking Agile means 'no documentation' or 'no planning'.
- Treating the Scrum Master as the team's boss.
- Extending a sprint to finish work (the sprint length is fixed).

activity.prompt: Sprint velocities were 18, 22 and 20 story points. Using the average, how many sprints are needed for a 150-point backlog? (round up)

quiz.q: The Agile Manifesto values working software over
quiz.why: The Agile Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation. It does not say documentation is worthless.
The Daily Scrum is time-boxed to 15 minutes.
The Product Owner is accountable for the Product Backlog and for ordering its items.
Kanban limits work in progress (WIP) in each stage. That exposes bottlenecks and improves flow.
Pair programming, two developers at one workstation, is an Extreme Programming (XP) practice.

scenes.text: Large online services deploy small changes many times a day without downtime.
Automated builds, tests and deployment pipelines make that safe.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
**DevOps:** culture and practices that unify development and operations — shared responsibility, automation, monitoring, fast feedback.
- **Continuous integration (CI):** merge to the main branch frequently; every commit triggers an automated build and tests.
- **Continuous delivery:** every change that passes the pipeline is releasable; deployment is a button press.
- **Continuous deployment:** passing changes go to production automatically.
- Supporting practices: infrastructure as code, containers, feature flags, blue-green and canary releases, observability (logs, metrics, traces). Common metrics: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate, time to restore service.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Pipeline stages
steps.body: Commit → build → unit tests → static analysis → integration tests → package container image → deploy to staging → acceptance tests → (manual approval in continuous delivery) → production canary (5% traffic) → full rollout.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Canary maths
steps.body: A canary gets 5% of 2,00,000 daily users = **10,000 users**. If its error rate is 2% versus 0.5% for the old version, the pipeline rolls back automatically before the other 1,90,000 users are affected.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing continuous delivery (releasable) with continuous deployment (released automatically).
- Thinking DevOps is just a job title or a tool.
- Running CI without fast, reliable tests.

activity.prompt: Order a typical CI/CD pipeline
items: Deploy to staging and run acceptance tests
Canary release to a small share of users

options: integrating code frequently with automated builds and tests
quiz.why: Continuous integration means merging code often and running automated builds and tests on each change, so integration problems show up early.

quiz.q: Continuous deployment differs from delivery because
quiz.why: In continuous deployment, every change that passes the pipeline is released to production automatically. In continuous delivery the release is a manual decision.

options: sends a new version to a small share of users first
quiz.why: A canary release exposes the new version to a small share of users first. If monitoring shows problems, it is rolled back before most users are affected.
Infrastructure as code defines servers and environments in versioned scripts. That makes setups reproducible and reviewable.

quiz.q: Which is a common DevOps metric?
quiz.why: Deployment frequency is one of the common DevOps (DORA) delivery metrics. Lines of comments and office size do not measure delivery.

questions.q: Software deteriorates due to
questions.why: Software does not wear out like hardware. It deteriorates because changes introduce defects.

questions.q: Waterfall phases are
questions.why: The waterfall model has phases that run one after another in a linear order.

questions.q: Scrum Sprint length
questions.why: A Scrum Sprint is time-boxed to one month or less.

questions.q: Spiral model is
questions.why: The spiral model repeats cycles, each starting with risk analysis. That makes it risk-driven.

questions.q: V-model pairs acceptance testing with
questions.why: The V-model pairs acceptance testing with the requirements phase at the top of the V.

questions.q: Agile Manifesto year
questions.why: The Agile Manifesto was written in 2001 at Snowbird, Utah.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Prototyping reduces requirements risk. Reason (R): Users react to something concrete and reveal real needs early. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Prototypes let users react to something concrete, which reveals real needs early and reduces requirements risk. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Case: an ISRO-style flight-control system needs strict verification at each level. Best fit
questions.why: Flight-control software needs strict verification at every level. The V-model pairs each design level with a matching test level.

questions.q: Velocities 24, 28, 26: backlog 130 points needs
questions.why: The average velocity is (24 + 28 + 26)/3 = 26 points. 130 / 26 = 5 sprints.

questions.q: Which is NOT a Scrum event?
questions.why: Scrum's events are the Sprint, Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review and Sprint Retrospective. A Gantt Review is not one.

questions.q: Case: testers are overloaded while developers keep starting new features. Kanban suggests
options: enforce WIP limits and swarm on testing
questions.why: Kanban says to enforce WIP limits and have everyone help clear the testing bottleneck first. Raising limits would only pile up more work.

questions.q: Continuous delivery vs deployment: in delivery the production release is
questions.why: In continuous delivery, every build is ready to release but the release to production is a manual, business decision. In deployment it is automatic.

questions.q: Canary at 2% of 5,00,000 users exposes
Which statement about Agile is FALSE?
questions.why: Agile values working software over comprehensive documentation, but it does not ban documentation. So the false statement is that it forbids all documentation.

questions.q: Which combination best suits a startup MVP with unknown requirements and a small co-located team?
options: Scrum/XP with short sprints and CI
questions.why: A startup MVP has unknown requirements and a small co-located team. Scrum/XP with short sprints and continuous integration gives fast feedback and lets the product change quickly. Yearly loops or a 12-month plan would be too slow.

questions.q: RAD relies heavily on
questions.why: Rapid Application Development delivers quickly using reusable components and strict time-boxes. It does not use long phases.

courses.title: Unit 2 · Requirements Engineering
courses.summary: Feasibility, elicitation techniques, functional and non-functional requirements, writing a good SRS, use cases and user stories with acceptance criteria, requirements validation, traceability and change management.
outcomes: Learners can classify requirements as functional or non-functional
Learners can write testable requirements and user stories with acceptance criteria
Learners can structure an SRS document
Learners can validate requirements and maintain a traceability matrix

story.title: What does the hospital really need?

scenes.text: A hospital asks for 'an app for appointments'. The receptionist, doctors and patients each want something different.
Requirements engineering turns vague wishes into agreed, testable statements.

steps.title: Process
steps.body:
Inception → **elicitation** → elaboration (analysis/modelling) → negotiation → **specification** → **validation** → management.
Elicitation techniques: interviews (structured/unstructured), questionnaires, workshops (JAD), **observation/ethnography**, document analysis, brainstorming, prototyping, scenarios.
**Feasibility study:** technical, economic (cost–benefit), operational, legal and schedule feasibility.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Pick a technique
steps.body:
- Hidden workflow habits of nurses → **observation**.
- 5,000 geographically spread customers → **questionnaire**.
- Conflicting department heads → facilitated **workshop**.
- Users unsure what screens they want → **prototype**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Economic feasibility
steps.body: System costs ₹40 lakh to build and ₹5 lakh/year to run; it saves ₹20 lakh/year. Net benefit per year = ₹15 lakh → simple payback ≈ 40 / 15 ≈ **2.7 years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Interviewing only managers, not real users.
- Treating the first stated solution ('an app') as the requirement.
- Skipping legal feasibility (privacy, data protection).

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the best elicitation technique

quiz.q: Which is NOT a feasibility type?
quiz.why: The standard feasibility types are technical, economic, operational (and often legal and schedule). Aesthetic is not one of them.
Ethnography means observing users in their real work setting. It reveals practices they may not think to mention.

quiz.q: Payback with cost 30, annual net benefit 10
quiz.why: Payback period = cost / annual net benefit = 30/10 = 3 years.
JAD is Joint Application Development, where users and developers work out requirements together in workshops.

quiz.q: The first step of RE is usually
quiz.why: Requirements engineering starts with inception, where the problem and stakeholders are understood at a basic level.

scenes.text: 'The app shall book an appointment' is a function. 'Booking shall complete within 2 seconds' is a quality.
Missing the second kind is how many systems fail in production.

steps.title: Types
steps.body:
- **Functional requirements:** what the system shall do (inputs, behaviour, outputs).
- **Non-functional requirements (quality attributes):** performance, reliability, availability, security, usability, maintainability, portability, scalability; plus constraints (platform, standards, legal).
- **Domain requirements** from the application area (e.g. tax rules).
Good requirements are **correct, unambiguous, complete, consistent, verifiable (testable), modifiable, traceable**, and ranked by importance.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classify
steps.body:
1. 'Users shall reset their password via OTP' → functional.
2. 'The system shall be available 99.9% of each month' → non-functional (availability).
3. 'All personal data shall be encrypted at rest' → non-functional (security).
4. 'The system shall generate GST invoices' → functional (domain-driven).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Make it testable
steps.body: Vague: 'The site should be fast.' → Testable: '95% of search requests shall return results within 1.5 s with 2,000 concurrent users on the production configuration.' 99.9% availability allows about **43.8 minutes** of downtime in a 730-hour month.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 'user-friendly', 'fast', 'robust' without measurable criteria.
- Mixing design decisions (use MySQL) into requirements without labelling them as constraints.
- Forgetting non-functional requirements entirely.

activity.prompt: Functional or non-functional?

items.text: Respond within 2 seconds for 95% of requests
Send an SMS when an order ships

quiz.why: Encrypting data at rest is about how well the system protects data, not what it does. So it is a non-functional (security) requirement.
A verifiable requirement is stated so it can be tested objectively and a clear pass or fail decided.

quiz.q: Downtime allowed by 99.9% availability in 1000 hours
quiz.why: 99.9% availability allows 0.1% downtime. 0.1% of 1000 hours = 1 hour.
User-friendly has no measurable meaning, so it cannot be tested. Add measures, such as a new user completes a task within 3 minutes.
Domain requirements come from rules of the application area, such as tax law for accounting software.

lessons.title: The SRS, use cases and user stories

scenes.text: Developers, testers, the client and the auditor all need the same picture of the system.
The Software Requirements Specification is that shared contract.

steps.title: SRS structure
steps.body: A typical SRS (in the style of IEEE 830, now superseded by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148): 1 Introduction (purpose, scope, definitions, references, overview) · 2 Overall description (product perspective, functions, user classes, constraints, assumptions) · 3 Specific requirements (functional, external interfaces, performance, design constraints, quality attributes) · appendices. Each requirement gets a unique ID.

steps.title: Use cases and user stories
steps.body:
**Use case:** actor, goal, preconditions, main success scenario (numbered steps), extensions/alternate flows, postconditions. UML use-case diagram shows actors and use cases with «include» and «extend» relationships.
**User story:** 'As a ⟨role⟩, I want ⟨goal⟩ so that ⟨benefit⟩', with **acceptance criteria** (often Given–When–Then). INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Use case
steps.body: Use case: Book appointment. Actor: Patient. Precondition: logged in. Main flow: 1 patient selects doctor; 2 system shows free slots; 3 patient picks a slot; 4 system confirms and sends SMS. Extension 3a: slot taken meanwhile → system shows updated slots. Postcondition: appointment stored.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · User story with criteria
steps.body:
As a patient, I want to cancel an appointment so that someone else can use the slot.
Given an appointment more than 2 hours away, when I tap Cancel and confirm, then the slot becomes free and I receive an SMS.
Given an appointment less than 2 hours away, when I tap Cancel, then I see a message to call the clinic.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing UI design details in a user story instead of the need.
- Use cases without alternate flows.
- Confusing «include» (always part of) with «extend» (optional/conditional).

activity.prompt: A good user story…
items: States a goal, not a UI design
Is small enough for one sprint
Can be estimated by the team

options: As a…, I want…, so that…
quiz.why: A user story is written as: As a [role], I want [goal], so that [benefit].
In use cases, «extend» adds optional or conditional behaviour to a base use case. «include» is for behaviour that is always performed.
INVEST stands for Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable. T is Testable.
IEEE 830 was replaced by ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, the standard for requirements engineering processes and products.

quiz.q: A use case's main success scenario is
options: numbered steps of the normal path
quiz.why: The main success scenario lists the numbered steps of the normal, successful path (the happy path). Alternative flows handle errors.

scenes.text: Six months after launch, an auditor asks: which tests prove requirement R-17?
A traceability matrix answers instantly.

steps.title: Practices
steps.body:
**Validation** — are we building the right product? Reviews/inspections, prototyping, test-case generation, model checking. (Verification asks: are we building the product right?)
**Traceability matrix:** links each requirement to design elements, code modules and test cases (forward and backward traceability).
**Change management:** change requests, impact analysis, change control board, baselines, versioned requirements.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Find the gap
steps.body: Matrix rows R1–R5; tests T1→R1, T2→R2, T3→R2, T4→R4. **R3 and R5 have no tests** → coverage gap. T3 duplicates R2 coverage (fine). A test linked to no requirement may indicate gold-plating or a missing requirement.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Impact analysis
steps.body: Change: 'support Hindi and Tamil'. Trace R-UI-* requirements → 14 screens, 3 report modules, 22 tests → estimate effort and risk before approving.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Confusing validation and verification.
- Updating code for a change without updating requirements and tests.
- Approving changes without impact analysis.

statements.s: Validation asks 'Are we building the right product?'
Verification asks 'Are we building the right product?'
A traceability matrix links requirements to tests.
Requirements never change after sign-off.
Impact analysis should precede approving a change.

quiz.why: Backward traceability links tests and code back to the requirements they come from. It answers why the item exists.

quiz.q: A requirement with no test indicates
quiz.why: A requirement with no test is not verified. It is a coverage gap.
A change control board reviews and approves or rejects change requests, to keep changes controlled.

quiz.q: Requirements reviews are a form of
quiz.why: Reviewing requirements with stakeholders checks that they describe the right product. That is validation.
A baseline is an approved, versioned snapshot that serves as a reference. Later changes follow change control.

questions.q: 'The system shall print invoices' is
questions.why: Printing invoices is something the system does, so it is a functional requirement.

questions.q: Validation checks
questions.why: Validation asks whether we are building the right product, as Boehm put it. Verification asks whether we are building the product right.

questions.q: User story parts
questions.why: A user story has a role (who), a goal (what) and a benefit (why).

questions.q: Which is non-functional?
questions.why: A response time of at most 2 s describes how well the system performs, not what it does. So it is non-functional.

questions.q: Observation is best for
questions.why: Observation shows what people really do, including tacit habits that they may not mention in interviews.

questions.q: INVEST's S
questions.why: In INVEST, S stands for Small, so the story fits within one sprint.

questions.q: Assertion (A): 'The system shall be fast' is a poor requirement. Reason (R): It cannot be objectively verified. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: The system shall be fast cannot be objectively verified, so it is a poor requirement. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: 99.95% monthly availability (730 h) allows downtime of about
Cost ₹60 lakh, annual savings ₹25 lakh, running cost ₹5 lakh: payback
questions.why: Net annual benefit = 25 − 5 = ₹20 lakh. Payback = 60/20 = 3 years.

questions.q: Case: a bank's app passes all tests but customers hate it because it doesn't fit their workflow. What failed?
questions.why: The app passes tests (it was built right) but does not fit the customers' workflow. So it is the wrong product, a validation failure.

questions.q: «include» vs «extend»: 'Pay bill' always performs 'Authenticate'. Relationship
questions.why: If Pay bill always performs Authenticate, the base use case includes it: Pay bill «include» Authenticate. «extend» is for optional behaviour.

questions.q: Traceability: 40 requirements, 34 have at least one test. Requirement test coverage
questions.why: Test coverage of requirements = 34/40 = 0.85, i.e. 85%.

questions.q: Which requirement is best written?
options: Passwords shall be stored using a salted, slow hash and locked after 5 failed attempts in 15 minutes
questions.why: The best requirement is specific and testable. It gives hashing, salt and a lockout rule with numbers. The others are vague.

questions.q: Gherkin acceptance criteria use
questions.why: Gherkin writes acceptance criteria in Given–When–Then form. This is common in behaviour-driven development.

questions.q: Ranking requirements with MoSCoW uses
questions.why: MoSCoW prioritises requirements as Must, Should, Could and Won't (this time).

questions.q: A test linked to no requirement may signal
questions.why: A test linked to no requirement may point to gold-plating (unneeded features) or a missing requirement. Investigate either way.

courses.title: Unit 3 · Project Planning, Estimation & Risk
courses.summary: Size metrics (LOC, function points), the COCOMO family, scheduling with work breakdown, Gantt charts, PERT and CPM, team organisation, and risk management — with worked numericals.

lessons.title: Size metrics: LOC and function points

scenes.text: Before quoting a price, a vendor must estimate the size of the software.
Counting lines is easy after coding; function points can be counted from requirements.

steps.title: LOC and FP
steps.body:
**LOC/KLOC:** simple, language-dependent, available only late.
**Function points (Albrecht/IFPUG):** count five components — External Inputs (EI), External Outputs (EO), External Inquiries (EQ), Internal Logical Files (ILF), External Interface Files (EIF) — weighted by complexity. Average weights: **EI 4, EO 5, EQ 4, ILF 10, EIF 7** (low/high: EI 3/6, EO 4/7, EQ 3/6, ILF 7/15, EIF 5/10).
UFP = Σ count × weight. **VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 × ΣFᵢ** over 14 general system characteristics rated 0–5 (so VAF ∈ [0.65, 1.35]). **FP = UFP × VAF**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · FP → effort
steps.body: If the organisation's productivity is 8 FP per person-month, 169 FP needs ≈ **21 person-months**; at ₹1.5 lakh per person-month the labour cost is ≈ ₹31.7 lakh.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using 1.35 + 0.01ΣF (the constant is 0.65).
- Counting the same file as both ILF and EIF.
- Comparing LOC across languages directly.

activity.prompt: Counts at average weights: 12 EI, 10 EO, 5 EQ, 3 ILF, 2 EIF; ΣFᵢ = 35. Function points?

quiz.why: In IFPUG function point counting, an internal logical file of average complexity has weight 10.
VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 × ΣFᵢ. With 14 characteristics rated 0–5, ΣFᵢ goes from 0 to 70, so VAF is 0.65 to 1.35.
IFPUG defines 14 general system characteristics, each rated 0 to 5.
Function points are based on requirements (inputs, outputs, files), so they can be estimated before any code exists.
Lines of code depend on the programming language, so the same functionality gives different LOC. That is a main weakness.

story.title: The estimate the client asks for

scenes.text: A client asks: how many person-months and how many calendar months for a 32 KLOC system?
Boehm's COCOMO gives a first answer from size and project type.

steps.title: Basic COCOMO (1981)
steps.body:
Effort **E = a × (KLOC)^b** person-months; development time **D = c × E^d** months; average staff = E / D.
| Mode | a | b | c | d |
- **Organic** (small team, familiar problem): 2.4, 1.05, 2.5, 0.38
- **Semi-detached:** 3.0, 1.12, 2.5, 0.35
- **Embedded** (tight constraints): 3.6, 1.20, 2.5, 0.32
**Intermediate COCOMO** multiplies by an Effort Adjustment Factor from 15 cost drivers. **COCOMO II** (2000) uses scale factors and works with FP or object points.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Same size, embedded
steps.body: E = 3.6 × 32^1.20 = 3.6 × 2^6 = 3.6 × 64 = **230.4 PM** — about 2.5× the organic effort, showing how constraints raise cost.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using LOC instead of KLOC.
- Thinking doubling the staff halves the time (Brooks' law: adding people to a late project makes it later).
- Applying organic coefficients to an embedded system.

activity.prompt: Basic COCOMO: input 'KLOC mode' (mode = organic, semidetached or embedded). Print effort in person-months rounded to 1 decimal.

kloc, mode = input().split()
kloc = float(kloc)

quiz.why: Basic COCOMO gives effort = a × (KLOC)^b, a power law, with constants by project mode.
The embedded mode has the largest exponent, b = 1.20 (organic 1.05, semi-detached 1.12).

quiz.q: Brooks' law says adding people to a late project
quiz.why: Brooks' law says adding people to a late project makes it later, because of training time and extra communication.

quiz.q: Development time D in organic mode
quiz.why: In organic mode, development time D = 2.5 × E^0.38, where E is the effort in person-months.
COCOMO II can use function points or object points as size measures, as well as lines of code.

lessons.title: Scheduling: WBS, Gantt, PERT and CPM

scenes.text: Caterer, tent, decorator and band each depend on others; some tasks can run in parallel.
The longest chain of dependent tasks decides the earliest possible finish — the critical path.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **WBS:** break the project into deliverables and work packages.
- **Gantt chart:** bars on a timeline; shows progress and overlaps.
- **CPM:** activity network with durations; forward pass (earliest start/finish), backward pass (latest start/finish); **slack (float) = LS − ES**; activities with zero slack form the **critical path**.
- **PERT:** three estimates — optimistic o, most likely m, pessimistic p: **tₑ = (o + 4m + p)/6**, **σ = (p − o)/6**; path variance = Σσ² (assuming independence).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · CPM
steps.body:
A (3 days) start; B (4) after A; C (2) after A; D (5) after B and C.
- Paths: A–B–D = 12, A–C–D = 10 → **critical path A–B–D, 12 days**.
- C: ES = 3, EF = 5; LS = 7 − 2 = 5 → **slack 2 days**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · PERT
steps.body: Task with o = 2, m = 4, p = 12 days: tₑ = (2 + 16 + 12)/6 = **5 days**; σ = 10/6 ≈ **1.67 days**. A path of three such tasks: mean 15 days, σ_path = √(3 × 1.67²) ≈ 2.89 days.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Picking the path with the most tasks instead of the longest duration.
- Using (o + m + p)/3 for PERT.
- Adding standard deviations instead of variances along a path.

activity.prompt: PERT estimates o = 3, m = 6, p = 15 days. Expected time tₑ?

quiz.why: The critical path is the longest-duration path through the network. It determines the minimum project length.
A critical activity has zero slack (float). Any delay on it delays the whole project.
In PERT, the standard deviation of an activity is σ = (p − o)/6, where p is the pessimistic and o the optimistic estimate.
A Gantt chart shows tasks as bars on a timeline.
WBS is Work Breakdown Structure, a hierarchical decomposition of the project into smaller tasks.

scenes.text: The lead developer might resign; the payment API might change; the client might add features.
Risk management lists such threats, ranks them and prepares responses.

steps.title: Risk management
steps.body:
Identify → analyse (probability × impact) → plan (avoid, mitigate, transfer, accept; contingency plans) → monitor.
**Risk exposure RE = P × loss.** Types: project risks (schedule, staff), technical risks (new tech, performance), business risks (market, strategy).
**RMMM:** risk mitigation, monitoring and management plan.
**Teams:** chief-programmer (hierarchical), democratic/egoless, mixed; Agile teams are cross-functional and self-managing. Communication paths in a team of n = n(n − 1)/2.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Risk exposure
steps.body: R1: key developer leaves, P = 0.3, loss ₹8 lakh → RE = **₹2.4 lakh**. R2: cloud costs overrun, P = 0.6, loss ₹2 lakh → RE = ₹1.2 lakh. Prioritise R1; mitigation: pair programming and documentation for knowledge sharing.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Communication paths
steps.body: Team of 5 → 10 paths; team of 10 → **45** paths — one reason large teams split into smaller squads.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ranking risks by impact alone.
- Listing risks once and never monitoring them.
- Assuming bigger teams always deliver faster.

activity.prompt: Choose the risk response

items.text: Drop an experimental framework for a proven one
Cross-train two developers on the billing module
Buy insurance / outsource hosting SLA penalties to a vendor
Note a tiny chance of a minor UI delay and do nothing
Add load testing early to reduce performance risk

quiz.why: Risk exposure = probability of the risk × loss if it happens.
Communication paths = n(n − 1)/2 = 8 × 7/2 = 28.
Insurance shifts the financial impact of a risk to a third party. That is risk transfer.
RMMM is the Risk Mitigation, Monitoring and Management plan.
A new, untested database technology is a technical risk, related to the technology used. Budget cuts and market changes are not technical.

questions.q: FP components count
questions.why: There are 5 function point components: External Inputs, External Outputs, External Inquiries, Internal Logical Files and External Interface Files.

questions.q: Critical path activities have slack
questions.why: Critical path activities have zero slack. Any delay to them delays the project.

questions.q: COCOMO was proposed by
questions.why: COCOMO was proposed by Barry Boehm in 1981.

questions.q: PERT tₑ for o = 1, m = 2, p = 9
questions.why: PERT expected time = (o + 4m + p)/6 = (1 + 8 + 9)/6 = 18/6 = 3.

questions.q: RE for P = 0.2, loss ₹10 lakh
questions.why: Risk exposure = 0.2 × ₹10 lakh = ₹2 lakh.

questions.q: VAF with ΣFᵢ = 0
questions.why: VAF = 0.65 + 0.01 × ΣFᵢ = 0.65 + 0 = 0.65, its minimum value.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Function points suit early estimation. Reason (R): They are derived from requirements rather than code. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Function points come from requirements (inputs, outputs, files), not from code. So they can be counted early. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: UFP: 5 EI (avg), 4 EO (avg), 2 ILF (avg)
questions.why: Average weights: EI 4, EO 5, ILF 10. So 5×4 + 4×5 + 2×10 = 20 + 20 + 20 = 60.

questions.q: Activities A(2), B(5) after A, C(3) after A, D(4) after C, E(2) after B and D. Project length
questions.why: Path A–C–D–E = 2 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 11 and path A–B–E = 2 + 5 + 2 = 9. The critical (longest) path gives the project length, 11.

questions.q: Case: a late project manager adds 6 new developers in the final month. Likely outcome per Brooks
questions.why: Brooks' law: adding people to a late project makes it later. The newcomers need training and add communication overhead, so there is further delay.

questions.q: Basic COCOMO semi-detached, 20 KLOC: effort ≈
questions.why: Semi-detached: effort = 3.0 × KLOC^1.12 = 3.0 × 20^1.12 ≈ 3.0 × 28.6 ≈ 86 person-months.

questions.q: Slack of B in the 11-day network above
questions.why: B starts at 2 and ends at 7, but E cannot start before 9. So B's latest start is 9 − 5 = 4 and the slack is 4 − 2 = 2.

questions.q: PERT path of tasks with σ = 2 and σ = 1.5: path σ
questions.why: Variances add along a path: σ² = 2² + 1.5² = 4 + 2.25 = 6.25. So σ = √6.25 = 2.5.

questions.q: FP: 20 EI (high), 10 ILF (low), ΣFᵢ = 70
Embedded COCOMO 1 KLOC effort
questions.why: Embedded basic COCOMO: effort = 3.6 × KLOC^1.2. For 1 KLOC, 1^1.2 = 1, so 3.6 PM.

questions.q: Communication paths grow
questions.why: Communication paths = n(n − 1)/2, which grows with the square of the team size.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Software Design, UML & Design Patterns
courses.summary: Design concepts (abstraction, modularity, information hiding), cohesion and coupling, architectural styles, UML class/sequence/state/activity diagrams, SOLID principles and common design patterns.
outcomes: Learners can rank cohesion and coupling types
Learners can choose an architectural style for a system
Learners can read and draw core UML diagrams
Learners can apply SOLID and recognise common GoF patterns

scenes.text: One drawer for spoons, another for knives: each has one clear purpose.
Modules should be organised the same way — high cohesion, low coupling.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.body:
Abstraction, **modularity**, **information hiding** (Parnas), functional independence, refinement, refactoring, separation of concerns.
**Cohesion** (inside a module), worst → best: coincidental, logical, temporal, procedural, communicational, sequential, **functional**.
**Coupling** (between modules), worst → best: **content**, common, external, control, stamp, **data** (and ideally no unnecessary coupling).
Goal: **high cohesion, low coupling**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classify cohesion
steps.body:
- A 'Utils' module with date formatting, file copy and email sending → **coincidental**.
- Init routine that opens the log, loads config and clears caches at startup → **temporal**.
- A function that reads a record, validates it, then computes its tax with each output feeding the next → **sequential**.
- `computeGST(amount)` doing exactly one thing → **functional**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Classify coupling
steps.body:
- Module A modifies B's internal variable directly → **content**.
- Both read/write a global config object → **common**.
- A passes a flag telling B which branch to run → **control**.
- A passes a whole Student record though B needs only the roll number → **stamp**.
- A passes just the roll number → **data** (best).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reversing the order of cohesion levels.
- Thinking zero coupling is achievable in a working system (modules must communicate).
- Confusing stamp coupling (whole structure) with data coupling (only needed items).

activity.prompt: Order cohesion from worst to best

quiz.why: Data coupling, where modules share only the data they need, is the loosest and best type. Content coupling is the worst.
Functional cohesion, where all parts do one well-defined task, is the best cohesion.
David Parnas advocated information hiding (1972) as a way to divide systems into modules.

quiz.q: Passing a flag to control another module's logic is
quiz.why: Passing a flag that tells another module what to do is control coupling.
Good design has high cohesion (each module does one thing) and low coupling (modules depend little on each other).

scenes.text: A city can be a single downtown, layered rings or many neighbourhoods linked by roads.
Software architecture makes the same big choices.

steps.title: Common styles
steps.body:
- **Layered** (presentation, business, data): separation of concerns; strict layering can add latency.
- **Client–server**, **n-tier**.
- **MVC / MVVM:** model, view, controller — UI separation.
- **Pipe-and-filter:** data flows through independent filters (compilers, Unix pipes, ETL).
- **Event-driven / publish–subscribe:** loose coupling via events (Kafka, message queues).
- **Microservices:** small independently deployable services owning their data; scalable and resilient but operationally complex (network calls, distributed transactions). Contrast **monolith**: simpler to start.
- **Repository / blackboard**, **peer-to-peer**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Match style to system
steps.body:
(a) Video transcoding (decode → resize → watermark → encode) → **pipe-and-filter**.
(b) A food-delivery platform scaling orders, payments and tracking separately → **microservices**.
(c) A college admission web app built by 3 students in a semester → **layered monolith** (MVC).
(d) Stock-price alerts to many subscribers → **publish–subscribe**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Microservice trade-off
steps.body: A request touches 4 services in sequence, each 99.9% available → end-to-end availability ≈ 0.999⁴ ≈ **99.6%**. Each hop also adds latency — so microservices need timeouts, retries and circuit breakers.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting a tiny project with dozens of microservices.
- Letting the view in MVC talk to the database directly.
- Thinking layered architecture forbids any optimisation shortcuts (relaxed layering exists).

activity.prompt: Match the system to an architectural style
pairs: Web UI with model, view, controller
Independently deployed services with own databases

options: own their data and deploy independently
quiz.why: Microservices are small services, each owning its data and deployable independently. They are not a single process with a shared database.
A compiler passes data through phases (lexing, parsing, ...) like filters connected by pipes. That is the pipe-and-filter style.

quiz.q: Availability of 3 services in series at 99% each
quiz.why: Services in series must all work, so availability multiplies: 0.99³ ≈ 0.970, about 97%.

options: UI from business data and control
quiz.why: MVC separates the user interface (view) from the business data (model) and the control logic. This is separation of concerns.
In event-driven systems, producers publish events without knowing who consumes them. That gives loose coupling.

scenes.text: Architects use blueprints; software teams use UML to sketch structure and behaviour.
UML 2.5 defines 14 diagram types — a handful cover most needs.

steps.title: Core diagrams
steps.body:
UML 2.5: **7 structural** (class, object, component, deployment, package, composite structure, profile) and **7 behavioural** (use case, activity, state machine, sequence, communication, timing, interaction overview).
**Class diagram relationships:** association (line, multiplicities like 1..*), **aggregation** (hollow diamond, whole–part, parts can exist alone), **composition** (filled diamond, parts die with the whole), **generalisation** (hollow triangle arrow), **realisation** (dashed line with hollow triangle), **dependency** (dashed arrow). Visibility: + public, − private, # protected, ~ package.
**Sequence diagram:** lifelines, messages in time order, activation bars, alt/loop fragments. **State machine:** states, transitions event[guard]/action. **Activity:** flow with decisions, forks/joins (parallelism).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Aggregation or composition?
steps.body:
- University – Department: departments are destroyed with the university → **composition**.
- Department – Professor: professors can exist without that department → **aggregation**.
- SavingsAccount is an Account → **generalisation**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · State machine
steps.body: Order states: Placed → (pay) → Paid → (ship) → Shipped → (deliver) → Delivered; from Placed or Paid → (cancel [before shipping]) → Cancelled. The guard [before shipping] blocks cancellation once Shipped.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Swapping the diamonds (filled = composition).
- Using sequence diagrams to show class structure.
- Forgetting multiplicities on associations.

activity.prompt: Match the UML notation

quiz.q: Number of diagram types in UML 2.5
quiz.why: UML 2.5 defines 14 diagram types: 7 structural and 7 behavioural.

quiz.q: Which shows message order over time?
quiz.why: A sequence diagram shows the messages between objects (lifelines) in time order.

quiz.q: Car–Engine where the engine is destroyed with the car (in the model)
quiz.why: If the engine is destroyed along with the car in the model, its lifetime is tied to the whole. That is composition.
Deployment diagrams show the hardware nodes and the software artefacts placed on them (the physical view).
In UML, # means protected visibility.

scenes.text: Experienced designers keep meeting the same problems: one shared logger, many notification channels, undoable commands.
Design patterns name proven solutions so teams can talk about them.

steps.title: SOLID
steps.body:
- **S**ingle responsibility: one reason to change.
- **O**pen/closed: open for extension, closed for modification.
- **L**iskov substitution: subtypes must be usable wherever the base type is expected.
- **I**nterface segregation: many small client-specific interfaces.
- **D**ependency inversion: depend on abstractions, not concretions (often via dependency injection).

steps.title: GoF patterns (23 in total)
steps.body:
**Creational (5):** Singleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype.
**Structural (7):** Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy.
**Behavioural (11):** Chain of Responsibility, Command, Interpreter, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Observer, State, Strategy, Template Method, Visitor.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Pick the pattern
steps.body:
- Old payment SDK has a different interface from your code → **Adapter**.
- Notify SMS, email and push listeners when an order ships → **Observer**.
- Swap discount algorithms at run time → **Strategy**.
- Undo/redo in an editor → **Command** (+ Memento for state).
- Add logging and caching around a service without changing it → **Decorator** or **Proxy**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · LSP violation
steps.body: Square extends Rectangle; code sets width = 5, height = 4 and expects area 20, but Square forces both sides equal → area 16 → **violates Liskov substitution**. Fix: don't model Square as a mutable subtype of Rectangle.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Overusing Singleton (hidden global state, hard to test).
- Confusing Adapter (change interface) with Decorator (add behaviour, same interface).
- Applying patterns where a simple function would do.

activity.prompt: Which GoF category?

quiz.why: The Gang of Four book describes 23 design patterns.

options: open for extension, closed for modification
quiz.why: The open/closed principle says software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

quiz.q: Pattern to make incompatible interfaces work together
quiz.why: The Adapter pattern wraps an object to make an incompatible interface fit the one the client expects.
Dependency inversion says to depend on abstractions (interfaces), not on concrete classes.
A Square that extends Rectangle cannot always replace a Rectangle without surprises. That violates the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP).

questions.q: Best cohesion
questions.why: Functional cohesion, where everything contributes to one task, is the best cohesion.

questions.q: Worst coupling
questions.why: Content coupling, where one module changes or relies on another's internals, is the worst coupling.

questions.q: Filled diamond in UML
questions.why: A filled diamond in UML means composition, a strong whole–part ownership.

questions.q: Pipe-and-filter fits
questions.why: Pipe-and-filter suits data-stream processing such as compilers and ETL pipelines.

questions.q: Observer pattern category
questions.why: Observer deals with how objects interact and communicate, so it is a behavioural GoF pattern.

questions.q: UML behavioural diagrams count
questions.why: UML has 14 diagram types, 7 of which are behavioural.

questions.q: Assertion (A): Microservices increase operational complexity. Reason (R): They introduce network calls, distributed data and many deployments. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Microservices add network calls, distributed data and many deployments to manage. That is why operational complexity grows. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Module that groups 'all printing functions' of unrelated reports is
questions.why: A module that groups printing functions for unrelated reports puts together things of the same category of action. That is logical cohesion, which is weak.

questions.q: End-to-end availability of 5 services in series at 99.9%
questions.why: Five services in series at 99.9% give 0.999⁵ ≈ 0.995, i.e. about 99.5%.

questions.q: Case: a class handles UI rendering, database access and email. Which principle is violated?
questions.why: A class that handles UI, database and email has many reasons to change. This violates the Single Responsibility Principle.

questions.q: Pattern for building a complex object step by step (e.g. a pizza order)
questions.why: The Builder pattern constructs a complex object step by step, such as a pizza order with many options.

questions.q: Adding retry and logging around an HTTP client without changing it, keeping the same interface
questions.why: A Decorator wraps an object with the same interface and adds behaviour such as retry and logging, without changing the original class.

questions.q: Passing an entire Employee object when only empId is needed is
questions.why: Passing a whole structure when only one field is needed is stamp coupling. Data coupling would pass only empId.

questions.q: Which is NOT a GoF structural pattern?
questions.why: Strategy is a behavioural pattern. Flyweight, Facade and Bridge are structural.

questions.q: Interface segregation recommends
questions.why: The Interface Segregation Principle says to prefer many small, role-specific interfaces over one big one.

questions.q: Communicational cohesion means elements
questions.why: In communicational cohesion, the parts of a module work on the same data.

courses.title: Unit 5 · Software Testing
courses.summary: Testing fundamentals, levels (unit, integration, system, acceptance), black-box techniques (equivalence partitioning, boundary value analysis, decision tables), white-box techniques (statement/branch/path coverage, cyclomatic complexity), regression, TDD and automation.
outcomes: Learners can design equivalence classes and boundary-value tests
Learners can compute cyclomatic complexity and independent paths
Learners can compare coverage criteria
Learners can plan integration and regression testing

scenes.text: A banking app rounds interest wrongly — found only after customers complain.
Testing at every level catches different kinds of defects earlier.

steps.title: Basics
steps.body:
**Error** (human mistake) → **fault/defect/bug** (in the artefact) → **failure** (observed wrong behaviour). Testing shows the presence of bugs, not their absence (Dijkstra). Exhaustive testing is impossible; defects cluster; early testing saves cost.
Levels: **unit** (single module, often by developers, with stubs/drivers), **integration** (interfaces: top-down with stubs, bottom-up with drivers, sandwich, big-bang), **system** (whole system against requirements, including performance, security, usability), **acceptance** (user/customer: alpha at developer site, beta at user site).
**Verification** (reviews, inspections, static analysis) complements **validation** (executing tests).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Stubs and drivers
steps.body: Top-down integration: main module M tested first; its called modules A, B not ready → replace them with **stubs** (simple fake implementations). Bottom-up: low-level module C tested first; a **driver** calls it with test data.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Which level?
steps.body:
- Checking that the GST function returns 18% correctly → unit.
- Payment service talks to bank API correctly → integration.
- 1,000 concurrent users can book tickets → system (performance).
- The hospital's staff try the system in a real ward → acceptance (beta).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling every problem a 'bug' (distinguish error, fault, failure).
- Big-bang integration on large systems (hard to localise faults).
- Thinking passing tests proves correctness.

activity.prompt: Match the term
pairs: Fake callee used in top-down integration
Fake caller used in bottom-up integration

quiz.why: Testing can show that bugs are present, but not that none are left (Dijkstra).
Beta testing is done by real users at their own site, in a real environment. Alpha testing is at the developer's site.
In top-down integration, higher modules are tested first. Stubs stand in for the missing lower modules.

quiz.q: Code reviews are a form of
quiz.why: Code reviews examine the code without running it (static). They check that the product is built correctly, so they are verification.

options: the whole integrated system against requirements
quiz.why: System testing checks the whole integrated system against the requirements, as end-to-end behaviour.

scenes.text: A form accepts ages 18 to 60. Testing every number is wasteful.
Pick representatives of each class and the edges where bugs hide.

steps.title: Techniques
steps.body:
- **Equivalence partitioning (EP):** split inputs into classes expected to behave alike (valid 18–60, invalid < 18, invalid > 60, non-numeric); test one value per class.
- **Boundary value analysis (BVA):** test at and around boundaries: min, min+1, nominal, max−1, max. For n independent variables, basic BVA needs **4n + 1** tests; robust BVA (adds min−1, max+1) needs **6n + 1**; worst-case BVA needs 5ⁿ.
- **Decision tables:** conditions × rules → actions; good for business rules.
- **State transition testing**, **cause–effect graphing**, **use-case testing**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · EP + BVA
steps.body:
Age valid 18–60.
- EP: classes {<18}, {18–60}, {>60} → e.g. 10, 35, 70.
- BVA (basic): 18, 19, 39, 59, 60.
- Robust BVA adds 17 and 61.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Decision table
steps.body: Loan approved if salary ≥ ₹30k AND credit score ≥ 700; if salary ≥ ₹30k but score < 700 → manual review; otherwise reject. Conditions: C1 salary ≥ 30k, C2 score ≥ 700. Rules: TT → approve; TF → review; FT → reject; FF → reject → **4 rules (2²)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Testing only valid classes.
- Forgetting invalid types (letters in a number field).
- Using 4n + 1 for robust BVA (it is 6n + 1).

activity.prompt: A function has 3 independent integer inputs, each with a range. How many test cases does basic boundary value analysis (4n + 1) require?

quiz.why: Equivalence partitioning divides inputs into classes that behave alike and tests one representative of each class.
Robust boundary value analysis tests min−, min, min+, nominal, max−, max, max+ for each variable: 6n + 1. For n = 2 that is 13.
Worst-case BVA takes every combination of the 5 values for each variable: 5ⁿ. For 2 variables, that is 25.

quiz.q: Decision table with 3 binary conditions has up to
quiz.why: A decision table with 3 binary conditions has 2³ = 8 possible combinations, so up to 8 rules.
Black-box testing derives tests from the specification, without looking at the code structure.

scenes.text: White-box testing looks inside the code and tries to drive down every branch.
Cyclomatic complexity tells how many independent paths there are.

steps.title: Coverage and McCabe
steps.body:
Coverage criteria (weak → strong): **statement** ⊂ **branch (decision)** ⊂ condition/decision and **MC/DC** (used in avionics) ⊂ multiple-condition; **path** coverage is strongest but often infeasible.
**Cyclomatic complexity V(G) = E − N + 2P** (edges, nodes, connected components) = **number of decision points + 1** (for single-entry, single-exit code; count each simple condition in compound predicates for a stricter measure) = number of regions in a planar flow graph. It gives the number of **linearly independent paths** = minimum tests for basis-path testing. V(G) > 10 is a common warning threshold.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Compute V(G)
steps.body: Flow graph with 9 edges and 7 nodes (one component): V = 9 − 7 + 2 = **4**. Code view: one if, one while and one if inside the loop → 3 decisions + 1 = **4** basis paths.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Statement vs branch
steps.body: `if (x > 0) y = 1; print(y);` One test with x = 5 executes every statement → 100% statement coverage, but the false branch (x ≤ 0, y unset) is never tried → only 50% branch coverage. A second test x = −1 reveals the bug.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using E − N + 1 (the formula has + 2P).
- Assuming 100% statement coverage means all branches were tested.
- Forgetting compound conditions (a && b) hide extra decisions.

activity.prompt: Approximate cyclomatic complexity of Python code read from standard input: count the decision keywords if, elif, for, while, and, or, except (as whole words) and add 1. Print the number.
activity.starter:
import sys, re
code = sys.stdin.read()
# count whole-word decision keywords with re.findall(r'\b(...)\b', code)
activity.solution:
import sys, re
code = sys.stdin.read()
words = re.findall(r'\b(if|elif|for|while|and|or|except)\b', code)
print(len(words) + 1)

quiz.q: V(G) = E − N + 2P with E = 12, N = 10, P = 1

quiz.why: Cyclomatic complexity V(G) is the number of linearly independent paths through the code. That is the size of the basis set of paths.

quiz.q: Strongest commonly required criterion in avionics
quiz.why: MC/DC (modified condition/decision coverage) is required for the most critical avionics software (DO-178C level A). It is stronger than statement coverage.
If every branch is executed, every statement on those branches is executed too. So 100% branch coverage implies 100% statement coverage, but not the other way round.

quiz.q: Code with 5 if statements (no loops, no compound conditions): V(G)
quiz.why: V(G) = number of decision points + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6.

story.title: A fix that broke something else

scenes.text: Fixing a tax bug silently broke invoice printing.
An automated regression suite would have caught it within minutes.

steps.title: Practices
steps.body:
- **Regression testing:** re-run tests after changes; select/prioritise tests by impact to save time.
- **Smoke testing** (does the build basically work?) vs **sanity testing** (narrow check after a fix).
- **Test automation pyramid:** many fast unit tests, fewer integration/API tests, few slow end-to-end UI tests.
- **TDD:** red (write a failing test) → green (minimal code to pass) → refactor.
- **Mutation testing:** inject small changes (mutants); a good suite 'kills' them. Mutation score = killed / (total − equivalent).
- Non-functional: load, stress, security (penetration), usability, accessibility testing.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Mutation score
steps.body: 100 mutants generated, 10 are equivalent (behave identically), tests kill 72 → score = 72 / 90 = **80%**.

steps.body: Red: test `assert gst(100) == 118` fails (function missing). Green: `def gst(a): return a * 1.18` → but floating result 118.00000000000001 fails an exact check → use rounding or integer paise. Refactor: extract the rate constant.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Automating only UI tests (slow, flaky).
- Writing production code before the test in TDD.
- Counting equivalent mutants against the score.

scenes.text: A government department compares two software vendors bidding for the same project.

steps.title: Quality models and SQA
steps.body:
**ISO/IEC 25010** product quality: functional suitability, performance efficiency, compatibility, usability (interaction capability in the 2023 revision), reliability, security, maintainability, portability (the 2023 revision also adds safety). Older: McCall's factors, ISO 9126.
**SQA activities:** standards, reviews (walkthroughs, formal inspections with roles: moderator, author, reader, recorder), audits, testing, defect tracking, metrics.
**Defect density** = defects / KLOC (or per FP).

steps.title: CMMI maturity levels
steps.body: 1 **Initial** (ad hoc, heroics) → 2 **Managed** (project-level planning and tracking) → 3 **Defined** (organisation-wide standard processes) → 4 **Quantitatively Managed** (statistical control) → 5 **Optimizing** (continuous improvement). ISO 9001 is a general quality-management standard also used by software firms.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Defect density
steps.body: Module A: 12 defects in 8 KLOC → **1.5 / KLOC**; module B: 9 defects in 3 KLOC → **3.0 / KLOC**. B deserves more review effort despite fewer defects.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Which CMMI level?
steps.body: Every project uses the company's standard tailored process, but there is no statistical control of process performance → **Level 3 (Defined)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing raw defect counts across modules of different sizes.
- Treating testing as the only SQA activity.
- Mixing up Managed (level 2) and Defined (level 3).

quiz.why: ISO/IEC 25010 is the product quality model, and maintainability is one of its characteristics.

scenes.text: A payment gateway promises 99.999% availability — about 5 minutes of downtime a year.
Reliability metrics make such promises measurable.

steps.title: Metrics
steps.body:
- **MTTF:** mean time to failure. **MTTR:** mean time to repair. **MTBF = MTTF + MTTR**.
- **Availability A = MTTF / (MTTF + MTTR)** = MTTF / MTBF.
- **ROCOF:** rate of occurrence of failures; **POFOD:** probability of failure on demand.
- With a constant failure rate λ (exponential model): reliability R(t) = e^(−λt), MTTF = 1/λ.
- Series system availability = product of availabilities; parallel (redundant) = 1 − Π(1 − Aᵢ).

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Redundancy
steps.body: Two servers each 99% available in parallel: A = 1 − 0.01² = **99.99%**. In series: 0.99² = **98.01%**. 99.999% availability allows about 0.00001 × 525,600 min ≈ **5.3 minutes** of downtime per year.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using MTTR in the numerator.
- Treating MTBF as equal to MTTF when repair time is significant.
- Multiplying availabilities for redundant (parallel) components.

activity.prompt: MTTF = 480 hours, MTTR = 20 hours. Availability in %?

quiz.why: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR: time to failure plus time to repair is one full cycle between failures.

quiz.q: Availability with MTTF 95 h and MTTR 5 h
quiz.why: Availability = MTTF/(MTTF + MTTR) = 95/100 = 95%.
In series, both must work, so availabilities multiply: 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, i.e. 81%.
In parallel, the system fails only if both fail: 1 − 0.1² = 0.99, i.e. 99%.
With a constant failure rate λ, MTTF = 1/λ = 1/0.001 = 1000 hours.

scenes.text: A cooperative bank's core system was written 15 years ago; the original team has left.
Most of a system's lifetime cost is maintenance — understanding, fixing, adapting and improving it.

steps.title: Types and practices
steps.body:
- **Corrective:** fix defects.
- **Adaptive:** adjust to a changed environment (new OS, new tax law, new API).
- **Perfective:** enhancements and performance/usability improvements requested by users.
- **Preventive:** improve maintainability to prevent future problems (refactoring, documentation).
Maintenance often accounts for the majority of total life-cycle cost (commonly cited as 60% or more).
**Re-engineering:** inventory analysis → document restructuring → **reverse engineering** (recover design from code) → code restructuring/refactoring → data restructuring → **forward engineering**. **Lehman's laws** (e.g. continuing change, increasing complexity) describe how evolving systems behave. **Technical debt:** shortcuts that make future change costlier.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classify
steps.body:
- Fix a crash when the PIN has a leading zero → corrective.
- Update for the new GST slab rules → adaptive.
- Add dark mode requested by users → perfective.
- Split a 3,000-line class and add tests, no new features → preventive.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Annual change traffic
steps.body: Maintenance effort ≈ ACT × development effort: if 15% of the code changes yearly (ACT = 0.15) and development took 200 PM → ≈ **30 PM/year** of maintenance (simple COCOMO-style estimate).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling all maintenance 'bug fixing'.
- Confusing reverse engineering (understand) with re-engineering (understand and rebuild).
- Ignoring technical debt until it blocks delivery.

scenes.text: Three developers edit the same project; a hotfix must go out today without half-finished features.

steps.title: SCM
steps.body:
**Software configuration management:** identify configuration items, version control, change control (requests, CCB), configuration status accounting, audits; **baselines** mark approved versions.
**Git** (distributed): working tree → `git add` (staging area) → `git commit` (local repository) → `git push` (remote). Branches are cheap pointers; `git merge` combines histories (may create a merge commit), `git rebase` replays commits on a new base (rewrites history — avoid on shared branches). Conflicts arise when the same lines change on both sides.
Branching strategies: trunk-based development (short-lived branches, feature flags), GitFlow (develop, feature, release, hotfix branches). **Semantic versioning:** MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Hotfix flow
steps.body: Production is at tag v2.3.0 on main. Create branch hotfix/otp from main, fix and test, merge into main, tag **v2.3.1** (PATCH bump), and also merge the fix into the development branch so it isn't lost.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Semantic versioning
steps.body: From 1.4.2: bug fix → **1.4.3**; new backward-compatible feature → **1.5.0**; breaking API change → **2.0.0**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rebasing commits already pushed to a shared branch.
- Committing secrets (API keys) to the repository.
- Forgetting to merge hotfixes back into the main development line.

In semantic versioning, a breaking API change increments MAJOR and resets the others: 3.2.1 becomes 4.0.0.

quiz.q: Rewriting shared history is risky with
quiz.why: git rebase rewrites commits. If they have already been pushed and others have them, histories diverge and cause trouble.
A baseline is an approved snapshot of configuration items that serves as a reference point. Later changes follow formal control.
Git is a distributed version control system. Every clone has the full history.

scenes.text: A class representative shares the internal marks spreadsheet in a public group by mistake. Everyone's marks are now visible.
Worse, the link allowed editing, and someone changed a few marks as a joke.
Then the file owner deleted it in panic, and on result day nobody could see the real marks at all.

steps.title: Three goals
steps.body:
- **Confidentiality**: only authorised people can read the information.
- **Integrity**: information is accurate and changed only by authorised people in authorised ways.
- **Availability**: authorised people can use the information and systems when they need them.

The hostel story broke all three: the leak (C), the edited marks (I), the deleted file (A).

steps.title: Matching controls to goals
steps.body:
- C: encryption, access permissions, 'view only' sharing.
- I: hashes and checksums, version history, digital signatures, change approval.
- A: backups, redundant servers, capacity planning, protection against overload.

steps.title: Beyond the triad
steps.body: Many frameworks add **authenticity** (it really came from who it claims), **non-repudiation** (the sender cannot deny sending it) and **accountability** (actions can be traced to a person through logs).

steps.title: Common mistake
steps.body: Thinking security means only secrecy. A hospital whose records are perfectly secret but unavailable during an emergency has failed at security.

steps.title: Balance
steps.body: Goals trade off. Very strict access helps confidentiality but can hurt availability. Good design finds the balance the business actually needs.
