quiz.why: (a + b)* means any number of a's and b's in any order, i.e. all strings over {a, b}.
r* means zero or more copies of r. That is ε plus r followed by r*, i.e. ε + rr*.

quiz.q: RE for strings with at least one b
quiz.why: A string with at least one b has some b with anything before and after. That is (a + b)*b(a + b)*.
In regular expressions, star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union.
∅* means zero repetitions of nothing, which gives only the empty string ε.

scenes.text: A compiler writer turns patterns into automata to scan code.
A theorist turns automata back into patterns to describe them.

steps.title: Conversions
steps.body:
- **RE → ε-NFA (Thompson):** build small NFAs for symbols and combine for union (new start with ε to both), concatenation (ε from first's accept to second's start), star (ε loops). Size linear in the RE.
- **FA → RE (state elimination):** turn edges into REs; eliminate states one by one: for p → q → r with self-loop s on q, add edge p → r labelled (p→q)(s)*(q→r).
- **Arden's theorem:** if P does not contain ε, the equation R = Q + RP has the unique solution **R = QP***.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Arden
steps.body:
DFA: q1 (start) with a-loop, q1 –b→ q2, q2 –a→ q1, q2 –b→ q2; final q2.
Equations: q1 = ε + q1a + q2a; q2 = q1b + q2b.
- q2 = q1b b* (Arden).
- q1 = ε + q1a + q1bb*a = ε + q1(a + bb*a) → q1 = (a + bb*a)*.
- q2 = (a + bb*a)* b b* → strings ending in b.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Thompson count
steps.body: For RE a(b + c)*: symbols a, b, c (2 states each), union adds 2, star adds 2, concatenation adds 0 new states → 6 + 2 + 2 = **10 states** in the standard Thompson construction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Arden when P contains ε (solution not unique).
- Forgetting the ε term for the start state.
- Eliminating the start or final state in state elimination (keep them).

activity.prompt: Arden's theorem: the solution of R = Q + RP (ε ∉ P) is R = ___

quiz.why: Thompson's construction builds an ε-NFA from a regular expression, using ε-moves to join pieces.
Arden's theorem says R = Q + RP has the unique solution R = QP* provided ε is not in P.
State elimination removes states one by one, replacing paths with regular expressions on the edges. It converts a finite automaton into a regular expression.
Arden's theorem with R = Q + RP, Q = b, P = a gives R = QP* = ba*.
Thompson's construction adds a constant number of states for each operator, so the NFA's size is linear in the length of the expression.

scenes.text: If two languages are regular, what about their union, intersection, complement?
Regular languages are closed under almost everything.

steps.title: Closure
steps.body:
Regular languages are closed under: union, intersection (product construction), **complement** (swap accepting states of a complete DFA), difference, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, quotient.
Not closed under infinite union (every language is a union of singletons).
**Decision problems** (all decidable): membership, emptiness (reachability of a final state), finiteness (cycle on a path from start to final), equivalence (minimise and compare, or test symmetric difference empty), subset.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Complement
steps.body: DFA for 'contains aa' (states 0, 1, 2 with 2 accepting and trapping). Complement: make 0 and 1 accepting, 2 non-accepting → accepts strings **without aa**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Using closure
steps.body: L = {w ∈ {a, b}* : #a(w) = #b(w)} is not regular. Proof using closure: if it were, L ∩ a*b* = {aⁿbⁿ} would be regular (intersection with a regular language) — contradiction.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Complementing an NFA by swapping states (must determinise first).
- Assuming a subset of a regular language is regular ({aⁿbⁿ} ⊆ a*b*).
- Claiming 'L1 ∪ L2 regular ⇒ both regular' (not necessarily).

activity.prompt: Is the result always regular when L1, L2 are regular?

quiz.q: Complement of a regular language is
quiz.why: The complement of a regular language is regular. Take a complete DFA and swap accepting and non-accepting states.

quiz.q: Emptiness of a DFA's language is
quiz.why: To check if a DFA's language is empty, test whether any accepting state is reachable from the start. That is a graph reachability check, so decidable.

quiz.q: Subset of a regular language is
quiz.why: A subset of a regular language need not be regular. For example, {aⁿbⁿ} is a subset of a*b*, which is regular.
A DFA's language is infinite exactly if there is a useful cycle: a cycle on a path from the start to an accepting state.
The intersection of two regular languages is regular, shown by the product DFA.

scenes.text: A DFA with p states reading a string of length ≥ p must revisit some state.
That loop can be pumped — repeated or skipped — and the string must stay in the language.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
If L is regular, there is p ≥ 1 such that every w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be split w = xyz with **|xy| ≤ p**, **|y| ≥ 1**, and **xyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0**.
To prove L non-regular (adversary game): assume p; **you** choose w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p; the adversary chooses any valid split; **you** choose i so that xyⁱz ∉ L. The lemma is necessary, not sufficient (some non-regular languages satisfy it).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · {aⁿbⁿ}
steps.body: Choose w = aᵖbᵖ. Since |xy| ≤ p, y = aᵏ with k ≥ 1. Pump i = 2: aᵖ⁺ᵏbᵖ has more a's than b's → ∉ L → **not regular**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Palindromes
steps.body: L = {w w^R}. Choose w = aᵖbbaᵖ. y lies within the first aᵖ. Pump i = 0: aᵖ⁻ᵏbbaᵖ is not a palindrome → **not regular**.

steps.title: Solved example 3 · {aⁿ² }
steps.body: Choose w = a^(p²). Pumping i = 2 gives length p² + k with 1 ≤ k ≤ p, and p² < p² + k ≤ p² + p < (p + 1)² → not a perfect square → **not regular**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a specific split yourself (you must handle every split).
- Using the lemma to prove a language *is* regular (it cannot).
- Picking w shorter than p.

activity.prompt: Order a pumping-lemma proof of non-regularity
items: Assume L is regular with pumping length p
Choose a string w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p
Consider every split w = xyz with |xy| ≤ p and |y| ≥ 1
Pick an i such that xyⁱz ∉ L
Conclude the contradiction: L is not regular

quiz.q: In the pumping lemma, |y| must be
quiz.why: In the pumping lemma, the pumped part y must be non-empty, |y| ≥ 1. Otherwise pumping would change nothing.
To show non-regularity you must handle every possible split xyz allowed by the lemma. The adversary picks the split, not you.
A DFA cannot count the a's unboundedly to match the b's. The pumping lemma shows {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular.
{aⁿbᵐ : n, m ≥ 0} is the language of a*b*, which is regular. There is no required relation between the counts.

quiz.q: Satisfying the pumping lemma proves regularity?
quiz.why: Satisfying the pumping lemma is only a necessary condition for regularity. Some non-regular languages also satisfy it, so it cannot prove regularity.

questions.q: (a + b)*abb denotes strings
questions.why: (a + b)*abb is any string followed by abb. So it denotes strings ending with abb.

questions.q: Regular languages are closed under complement?
questions.why: Regular languages are closed under complement: complete the DFA and swap the accepting states.

questions.q: Arden: R = Q + RP solution
questions.why: By Arden's theorem, the solution of R = Q + RP is R = QP*, when ε is not in P.

questions.q: RE for strings of odd length over {a, b}
questions.why: Odd length means one symbol followed by any number of pairs. That is (a + b)((a + b)(a + b))*.

questions.q: {aⁿ : n is prime} is
questions.why: The set of prime lengths cannot be pumped. By the pumping lemma, {aⁿ : n prime} is not regular.

questions.q: (a*b*)* equals
questions.why: (a*b*)* can produce any string of a's and b's, since any string is a sequence of a-blocks and b-blocks. So it equals (a + b)*.

questions.q: Assertion (A): {aⁿbⁿ} is not regular. Reason (R): A DFA cannot count unboundedly. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: A DFA has finite memory and cannot count unboundedly, so it cannot match the a's and b's. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Which is regular?
questions.why: {aⁿbᵐ : n + m even} only depends on the parity of the total length, so a finite automaton can handle it. {aⁿbⁿ}, {ww} and {#a = #b} need unbounded counting or memory.

questions.q: RE for binary strings not containing 11
questions.why: Strings without 11 have every 1 followed by 0, except possibly a final 1. That is (0 + 10)*(ε + 1).

questions.q: Case: a validator must accept balanced parentheses of any depth. Can a regex (in the formal sense) do it?
options: no — the language is not regular
questions.why: Balanced parentheses of any depth need a stack to count open brackets. The language is not regular, so no formal regular expression can match it.

questions.q: {aᵐbⁿ : m ≠ n}
questions.why: If {aᵐbⁿ : m ≠ n} were regular, its complement within a*b* would be regular, and that complement is {aⁿbⁿ}, which is not regular. So it is not regular.
{a^(2n)} is (aa)*, which is regular. Adding the single string b gives (aa)* + b, still regular.

questions.q: Minimal DFA states for (a + b)*a(a + b)
questions.why: The DFA must remember the last two symbols, since the second-last must be a. There are 4 combinations, so 4 states.

questions.q: If L1 is regular and L1 ∩ L2 is non-regular, then L2 is
questions.why: If L2 were regular, then L1 ∩ L2 would be regular as well, since regular languages are closed under intersection. So L2 must be non-regular.
The DFA tracks (#a − #b) mod 3, which needs only 3 states. So the language is regular.

questions.q: Which language satisfies the pumping lemma yet is non-regular (a known example type)?
options: {a^i b^j c^k : i = 0 or j = k}
questions.why: The language {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = 0 or j = k} is non-regular but still satisfies the pumping lemma. It is the classic example that the lemma's converse is false.

scenes.text: 'The cat sat' = noun phrase + verb phrase; a noun phrase = article + noun.
Programming languages are defined the same way — by context-free grammars.

steps.title: Definitions
steps.body:
CFG G = (V, T, P, S): variables, terminals, productions A → α (α ∈ (V ∪ T)*), start S. **Leftmost / rightmost derivations**; a **parse tree** has S at the root, terminals at the leaves (the yield). L(G) = strings of terminals derivable from S.
Every regular language is context-free (right-linear grammars).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Classic grammars
steps.body:

A CFG is **ambiguous** if some string has two distinct parse trees (equivalently two leftmost derivations). Some CFLs are **inherently ambiguous** (every grammar is ambiguous), e.g. {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k}. Deciding whether an arbitrary CFG is ambiguous is **undecidable**.

steps.title: Algorithm
steps.body:
Grammar in CNF, input w = a₁…aₙ. Table T[i][j] = set of variables deriving aᵢ…aⱼ.
- Length 1: T[i][i] = {A : A → aᵢ}.
- Length ℓ > 1: for every split k, if B ∈ T[i][k] and C ∈ T[k+1][j] and A → BC, add A to T[i][j].
Accept iff S ∈ T[1][n]. Time **O(n³ · |G|)**. Shows CFL membership is decidable (in polynomial time).

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
PDA P = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, Z₀, F) with δ: Q × (Σ ∪ {ε}) × Γ → finite subsets of Q × Γ*. A move reads an input symbol (or ε), pops the top stack symbol and pushes a string.
Instantaneous description (q, remaining input, stack). Acceptance **by final state** or **by empty stack** — equivalent for nondeterministic PDAs. NPDAs accept exactly the CFLs.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · PDA for {aⁿbⁿ : n ≥ 1}
steps.body:
- δ(q0, a, Z₀) = (q0, aZ₀); δ(q0, a, a) = (q0, aa) — push each a
- δ(q0, b, a) = (q1, ε); δ(q1, b, a) = (q1, ε) — pop for each b
- δ(q1, ε, Z₀) = (q2, Z₀), q2 final.
Trace aabb: push, push, pop, pop, see Z₀ → accept. aab ends with a on the stack → reject.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · {w c w^R}
steps.body: Push symbols until c, then switch state and pop matching symbols; accept when Z₀ is exposed. Deterministic because the centre marker c tells the PDA when to switch. Without the marker ({w w^R}) the PDA must **guess** the middle — nondeterminism is essential.

steps.body: Push a's, pop one per b; at the end accept if no b is left unmatched (stack may still hold a's): final-state acceptance makes this easy.

steps.title: Equivalence
steps.body:
**CFG → PDA:** one-state PDA: push S; if top is a variable A, replace it by the RHS of some rule (ε-move); if top is a terminal, match it with the input and pop. Accept by empty stack. This simulates leftmost derivations.
**PDA → CFG:** variables [p X q] meaning 'from p, consuming input, pop X and reach q' (triple construction).
**DPDA:** at most one move in every situation. DCFLs (accepted by DPDAs by final state) ⊂ CFLs strictly; e.g. {ww^R} is a CFL but not a DCFL. Every DCFL has an unambiguous grammar; LR(k) grammars generate exactly the DCFLs.

steps.title: Statement
steps.body:
If L is context-free, there is p such that every w ∈ L with |w| ≥ p can be written w = uvxyz with **|vxy| ≤ p**, **|vy| ≥ 1**, and **uvⁱxyⁱz ∈ L for all i ≥ 0**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · {ww}

steps.title: Closure
steps.body:
CFLs are **closed** under union, concatenation, Kleene star, reversal, homomorphism, inverse homomorphism, substitution, and **intersection with a regular language**.
**Not closed** under intersection and complement: {aⁿbⁿcᵐ} ∩ {aᵐbⁿcⁿ} = {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}. (Complement fails because intersection = complement of union of complements.)
DCFLs: closed under complement and intersection with regular; not under union, intersection, concatenation.

steps.title: Decision problems
steps.body:
Decidable for CFGs: **membership** (CYK), **emptiness** (generating symbols), **finiteness** (cycles in the dependency graph of a simplified grammar).
Undecidable: **equivalence** of two CFGs, **ambiguity**, **L(G) = Σ*** (universality), whether L(G) is regular, whether L(G1) ∩ L(G2) = ∅.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Intersection with regular

- Forgetting CFL ∩ regular is CFL.

story.title: A clerk with an endless notebook

steps.title: Definition
steps.body:
TM M = (Q, Σ, Γ, δ, q₀, B, F) with δ: Q × Γ → Q × Γ × {L, R} (partial). The tape is infinite (to the right, or both ways); B is blank.
On input w the machine may **accept** (enter an accepting/halting state), **reject**, or **loop forever**.
**Decider** = TM that halts on every input. A language is **recursive (decidable)** if some decider accepts it; **recursively enumerable (RE)** if some TM accepts exactly its strings (possibly looping on others).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · TM for {aⁿbⁿ}
steps.body: Repeat: mark the leftmost a as X, move right to the first b, mark it Y, move back left to the leftmost unmarked a. When no a remains, scan to check only Y's remain (no unmarked b) → accept. Each round is O(n) moves → O(n²) total.

steps.title: Equivalent models
steps.body:
- **Multi-tape TM:** simulated by a single-tape TM with at most **quadratic** slowdown.

steps.title: Hierarchy
steps.body:
- **Type 3** regular grammars ↔ finite automata
- **Type 2** context-free ↔ PDAs
- **Type 1** context-sensitive (|α| ≤ |β| rules) ↔ **linear bounded automata** (TM restricted to the input length)
- **Type 0** unrestricted ↔ TMs (RE languages)
Inclusions: Regular ⊂ CFL ⊂ CSL ⊂ Recursive ⊂ RE ⊂ all languages (each strict).

steps.title: Closure facts
steps.body:
- Recursive languages: closed under union, intersection, complement, concatenation, star.
- RE languages: closed under union, intersection, concatenation, star; **not under complement**.
- **L is recursive ⇔ L and its complement are both RE.**

- Complement of the halting set: **not RE**.

scenes.text: A startup promises a tool that tells whether any program will finish or loop forever.
Turing proved in 1936 that no such tool can exist for all programs.

steps.title: Diagonalisation proof
steps.body:
HALT = {⟨M, w⟩ : M halts on w}. Suppose a decider H exists. Build D: on input ⟨M⟩, run H(⟨M, ⟨M⟩⟩); if H says 'halts', **loop forever**; else **halt**. Now run D on ⟨D⟩: if D halts on ⟨D⟩, then H said it doesn't halt… contradiction either way. So **HALT is undecidable**.
HALT (and A_TM = {⟨M, w⟩ : M accepts w}) are **RE** (simulate M) but not recursive; their complements are **not RE**.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Why simulating doesn't decide
steps.body: Running M on w and waiting works when M halts, but if M loops we wait forever and can never answer 'no'. That's semi-decidability.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Counting argument
steps.body: There are countably many TMs (finite descriptions) but uncountably many languages over Σ (subsets of Σ*). So **most languages are not even RE**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking the halting problem is undecidable only for big programs (it is about a general algorithm for all programs).
- Saying HALT is not RE (it is RE; its complement is not).
- Confusing 'undecidable' with 'hard but solvable'.

scenes.text: To show a new problem is impossible, show that solving it would solve the halting problem.
Rice's theorem kills a whole family of questions at once.

steps.title: Reductions
steps.body:
A **mapping reduction** A ≤ₘ B is a computable f with w ∈ A ⇔ f(w) ∈ B.
- If A ≤ B and B is decidable → A decidable.
- If A ≤ B and A is undecidable → **B undecidable**.
- If A ≤ B and A is not RE → B not RE.
Typical: reduce A_TM or HALT to the new problem.

steps.title: Rice's theorem
steps.body:
Every **non-trivial property of the language** recognised by a TM is undecidable. (Non-trivial: some RE languages have it, some don't; property of L(M), not of M's code.) Examples: Is L(M) empty? finite? regular? contains 'abc'? equal to Σ*? — all undecidable.
Rice does **not** apply to properties of the machine itself, like 'M has more than 5 states' (decidable) or 'M moves left on input ε within 100 steps' (decidable by simulation).

steps.title: Solved example 1 · E_TM
steps.body: E_TM = {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅}. Non-trivial language property → **undecidable** by Rice. Its complement (L(M) ≠ ∅) is **RE** (dovetail all inputs), so E_TM is **not RE**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Decidable or not?
steps.body:
- 'Does M halt on ε within 1000 steps?' → **decidable** (simulate 1000 steps).
- 'Is L(M) regular?' → **undecidable** (Rice).
- 'Does M have an even number of states?' → **decidable** (syntax).
- 'Does M accept 0101?' → undecidable (reduce A_TM).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Applying Rice to machine properties rather than language properties.
- Reducing in the wrong direction (reduce the *known hard* problem to the new one).
- Forgetting trivial properties (true for all RE languages) are decidable.

quiz.why: If A reduces to B and A is undecidable, B cannot be decidable, otherwise A would be decidable too. So B is undecidable.
Rice's theorem is about non-trivial semantic properties, i.e. properties of the language L(M) a machine accepts, not of its code.
Whether L(M) = Σ* is a non-trivial property of the language, so by Rice's theorem it is undecidable.
'M has 7 states' is a property of the machine's description, not of its language. You can just count the states, so it is decidable.
E_TM (is L(M) empty?) is not RE, but its complement is RE: search for any accepted string. So E_TM is co-RE but not RE.

lessons.title: Undecidable problems beyond TMs: PCP and grammars

scenes.text: You get domino types with strings on top and bottom. Can you line some up so the top and bottom read the same?
No algorithm can always answer — the Post Correspondence Problem.

steps.title: PCP and consequences
steps.body:
**PCP:** given pairs (tᵢ, bᵢ), is there a sequence i₁…iₖ (k ≥ 1) with t_{i₁}…t_{iₖ} = b_{i₁}…b_{iₖ}? **Undecidable** (but RE: search all sequences). Over a one-letter alphabet it is decidable.
PCP reductions show undecidability of: CFG ambiguity, emptiness of the intersection of two CFLs, CFG equivalence/universality.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · A PCP instance with a solution
steps.body: Dominoes: 1 = (a, ab), 2 = (b, ca), 3 = (ca, a), 4 = (abc, c). Sequence 1, 2, 3, 1, 4: top a·b·ca·a·abc = abcaaabc; bottom ab·ca·a·ab·c = abcaaabc ✓ → **match**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Summary table
steps.body:
Regular (DFA): membership, emptiness, finiteness, equivalence — all decidable.
CFL (CFG): membership, emptiness, finiteness decidable; equivalence, universality, ambiguity, intersection-emptiness undecidable.
RE (TM): membership semi-decidable; emptiness, finiteness, equivalence undecidable.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking PCP is undecidable even with one letter (unary PCP is decidable).
- Saying CFL emptiness is undecidable (it is decidable).
- Forgetting that PCP solutions may reuse dominoes.

story.title: Easy to check, hard to find

scenes.text: Checking a finished Sudoku takes seconds; solving a giant one may take ages.
Whether 'easy to check' implies 'easy to solve' (P = NP?) is a famous open problem.

steps.title: Classes
steps.body:
- **P:** decision problems solvable by a deterministic TM in polynomial time.
- **NP:** solvable in polynomial time by a nondeterministic TM ⇔ a 'yes' certificate can be **verified** in polynomial time.
- **NP-hard:** every NP problem reduces to it in polynomial time. **NP-complete:** NP-hard and in NP.
- **Cook–Levin:** SAT is NP-complete. 3-SAT, CLIQUE, VERTEX-COVER, INDEPENDENT-SET, HAMILTONIAN-CYCLE, TSP (decision), SUBSET-SUM, 3-COLOURING are NP-complete. 2-SAT, shortest path, MST, bipartite matching are in P.
- P ⊆ NP; whether P = NP is open. If any NP-complete problem is in P, then P = NP.
- Halting problem is NP-hard (and undecidable) but not in NP.

steps.title: Solved example 1 · Showing a problem is NP-complete
steps.body: INDEPENDENT-SET: (1) in NP — certificate = set of k vertices; check no edge inside in O(k²). (2) NP-hard — reduce from CLIQUE: G has a clique of size k ⇔ the complement graph has an independent set of size k. Both steps → **NP-complete**.

steps.title: Solved example 2 · Vertex cover ↔ independent set
steps.body: In a graph with n vertices, S is a vertex cover ⇔ V − S is an independent set. So a minimum vertex cover of size c means a maximum independent set of size n − c.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reducing the new problem *to* a known NP-complete problem (wrong direction for hardness).
- Saying NP means 'not polynomial' (it means nondeterministic polynomial).
- Claiming 2-SAT is NP-complete.

steps.title: Closure
steps.body:
- Regular: ∪ ∩ complement · * reversal h h⁻¹ — all yes
- CFL: ∪ · * reversal h ✓; ∩ ✗; complement ✗; ∩ regular ✓
- DCFL: complement ✓, ∩ regular ✓; ∪ ✗, ∩ ✗, · ✗

steps.title: Decidability
steps.body:

quiz.why: A DFA must remember the last four symbols, 2⁴ = 16 combinations. So it needs 16 states.

scenes.text: Ten languages, classify each as fast as you can.
Then check the reasons.

steps.title: Drill set
steps.body:
1. {aⁿbᵐ : n, m ≥ 0} → regular (a*b*)
2. {aⁿbⁿ : n ≤ 100} → regular (finite)
3. {aⁿbⁿ} → DCFL, not regular
4. {aⁿbⁿcⁿ} → CSL, not CFL
5. {ww^R} → CFL, not DCFL
6. {ww} → CSL, not CFL
7. {a^p : p prime} → CSL (recursive), not CFL
8. {⟨M⟩ : M halts on ε} → RE, not recursive
9. {⟨M⟩ : L(M) = ∅} → not RE (co-RE)
10. {w : #a = #b} → DCFL (a counter suffices; deterministic), not regular

steps.title: Proof patterns
steps.body:
- Non-regular: pumping lemma, Myhill–Nerode, or closure (intersect with a regular set to get a known non-regular language).
- Non-CFL: CFL pumping lemma or intersect with a regular set to get {aⁿbⁿcⁿ}.
- Undecidable: reduce A_TM/HALT, or Rice.

steps.title: Speed rule
steps.body: Ask in order: is it finite? can a DFA do it (bounded memory)? one stack enough? needs comparisons of three counts or copies? is it about TM behaviour?

activity.prompt: Classify each language (tightest class)

quiz.why: Limiting n to at most 100 makes the language finite. Every finite language is regular.
A PDA can count the difference between a's and b's on its stack. So {w : #a = #b} is context-free.
The set of prime lengths is not regular, and a unary CFL must be regular, so it is not context-free. It is still decidable by testing primality.
Emptiness of L(M) is not RE. Its complement (nonemptiness) is RE, and E_TM is undecidable. So it is co-RE but not RE.
{ww} requires comparing two halves of arbitrary strings, which a single stack cannot do. It is not context-free.

steps.title: Method
steps.body:
- For 'minimum DFA states' questions: list Myhill–Nerode classes.
- For 'which is CFL' questions: try to describe a PDA in one sentence; if you need two independent counters compared with a third, it's not CFL.
- For decidability: identify the model (DFA/CFG/TM) first.

steps.title: Mark-losing habits
steps.body:
- Forgetting dead states in DFA counts
- Mixing up CFL and DCFL closure
- Applying Rice to syntactic properties

steps.title: Why this matters
steps.body: Regex engines, lexers and parsers (compilers), protocol verification, and limits of static analysis and AI code checkers all rest on these results.

quiz.q: Minimal DFA questions are best handled by
quiz.why: For minimal DFA questions, count Myhill–Nerode equivalence classes. The number of classes is the number of states in the minimal DFA.

quiz.q: Two independent counters compared with a third suggests
quiz.why: Comparing two counters with a third needs more than one stack, so the language is not context-free.

quiz.q: Static analysers can never be both sound and complete for all programs because of
quiz.why: By Rice's theorem, non-trivial semantic properties of programs are undecidable. So no analyser can be both sound and complete for all programs.
Lexers recognise tokens, which are regular, so regular expressions and DFAs are used.
Compiler parsers use deterministic grammars (LR or LL), which handle the deterministic context-free languages efficiently.

questions.q: [Paper A] NFA → DFA conversion uses
questions.why: Converting an NFA to a DFA uses the subset construction. Each DFA state is a set of NFA states.

questions.q: [Paper A] Regular languages are closed under
questions.why: Regular languages are closed under complement, and under all Boolean operations.

questions.q: [Paper A] PDA = FA +
questions.why: A pushdown automaton is a finite automaton plus a stack.

questions.q: [Paper A] CNF derivation length for n = 8
questions.why: A CNF derivation of a string of length n takes 2n − 1 steps. For n = 8 that is 15.

questions.q: [Paper A] {ww^R} is
questions.why: {ww^R} (even palindromes) is context-free. A PDA can guess the middle and match with a stack.

questions.q: [Paper A] RE closed under complement?
questions.why: RE languages are not closed under complement. The complement of the halting language is not RE.

questions.q: [Paper A] Assertion (A): CFG equivalence is undecidable. Reason (R): It can be reduced from PCP/universality. Choose:
options: Both true, R does not explain A
questions.why: Equivalence of CFGs is undecidable, shown through reductions from PCP or universality. Both are true and the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: [Paper A] 2-SAT vs 3-SAT
questions.why: 2-SAT can be solved in polynomial time, but 3-SAT is NP-complete.

questions.q: [Paper A] Every CSL is
questions.why: Every context-sensitive language is decided by an LBA, which can be made to halt. So CSLs are recursive.

questions.q: [Paper A] Which is NOT closed for CFLs?
questions.why: CFLs are not closed under complement (or intersection). They are closed under union, star and reversal.

questions.q: [Paper B] Minimal DFA for binary strings with value ≡ 0 mod 6
questions.why: δ(r, b) = (2r + b) mod 6. Residues 1 and 4 have identical transitions (both non-accepting), as do 2 and 5; 0 (accepting) and 3 have the same transitions but differ in acceptance → classes {0}, {3}, {1, 4}, {2, 5} → 4 states.

questions.q: [Paper B] DFA states for strings over {a, b} containing 'aba'
questions.why: The DFA tracks progress towards aba: no progress, a, ab, found aba. That is 4 states.

questions.q: [Paper B] RE for strings over {0,1} with no two consecutive 0s
questions.why: No two consecutive 0s means each 0 is followed by 1, except possibly the last symbol. That is (1 + 01)*(ε + 0).

questions.q: [Paper B] {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i + j = k}
questions.why: A PDA pushes a symbol for each a and each b, then pops one for each c. The condition i + j = k can be checked with one stack, so it is context-free.

questions.q: [Paper B] {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j and j = k}
questions.why: Requiring i = j = k gives the language aⁿbⁿcⁿ, which is not context-free.

questions.q: [Paper B] Parse trees for id+id+id+id+id under E → E + E | id
questions.why: The number of parse trees for n + 1 ids under E → E + E | id is the Catalan number Cₙ. For 5 ids, C₄ = 14.

questions.q: [Paper B] 'Does M accept at least one palindrome?'
questions.why: Whether L(M) contains a palindrome is a non-trivial property of the language. By Rice's theorem it is undecidable.

questions.q: [Paper B] 'Does M on ε visit state q within 50 steps?'
questions.why: Simulate M on ε for 50 steps and see if it visits q. This is a bounded simulation, so it is decidable.

questions.q: [Paper B] NFA with n states → DFA reachable states at most
questions.why: The subset construction gives states that are subsets of the n NFA states. So at most 2ⁿ reachable states.

questions.q: [Paper B] L recursive, L' its complement: L' is
questions.why: Recursive languages are closed under complement. Swap the accept and reject answers of the decider.

An **element** is usually an opening tag, content and a closing tag: `

steps.title: The HTML5 skeleton
steps.body:
Every page should start with:

- `<!DOCTYPE html>` — tells the browser to use standards mode.
- `<html lang='en'>` — the root element; `lang` helps screen readers and search engines.

steps.title: Form anatomy
steps.body:
`<form action='/submit' method='post'>` groups controls. Each control needs a `name` (the key sent to the server).

- `method='get'` puts data in the URL query string — fine for searches.
- `method='post'` sends data in the request body — use for changes and private data.
- `<label for='email'>` connects to `<input id='email'>`; clicking the label focuses the input and screen readers announce it.

steps.title: Input types and built-in validation
steps.body:
Types: `text`, `email`, `password`, `number`, `date`, `tel`, `checkbox`, `radio`, `file`, `range`. Other controls: `<select>`, `<textarea>`, `<button>`.

Validation attributes: `required`, `min`, `max`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `pattern`, `step`. Radio buttons with the same `name` form one group.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Age field 18–60.** Step 1: `type='number'`. Step 2: `min='18' max='60'`. Step 3: `required`. Result: `<input type='number' name='age' min='18' max='60' required>`.

**Example 2. Gender radio group.** Step 1: give both radios `name='g'`. Step 2: distinct `value`s. Step 3: wrap each in a label. Only one can be selected because they share a name.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Trusting browser validation alone: anyone can bypass the browser, so the **server must validate again**.
- Using placeholder instead of label (placeholders disappear and are not reliable labels).
- Sending passwords with GET (they end up in URLs and logs).
- Forgetting `name`, so the field is never submitted.

quiz.why: Users can disable or bypass client-side checks, so the server must validate again. Never trust input from the client.

quiz.q: Radio buttons form a group when they share the same…

story.title: Why is my button still blue?

scenes.text: Neha writes `.btn { color: red }` but the button stays blue.
DevTools shows `#nav a { color: blue }` wins because an id selector is more specific.

steps.title: Selector types
steps.body:
- Type `p`, class `.btn`, id `#nav`, universal `*`, attribute `[type='email']`.
- Combinators: descendant `nav a`, child `ul > li`, adjacent sibling `h2 + p`, general sibling `h2 ~ p`.
- Pseudo-classes `:hover`, `:focus`, `:nth-child(2n)`; pseudo-elements `::before`, `::after`.

steps.title: The cascade order
steps.body:
When rules conflict the browser compares, in order:

- **Origin and importance** (`!important` user/author declarations).
- **Specificity** written as (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements). Inline style beats all selectors.
- **Source order** — the later rule wins on a tie.

Some properties (color, font) **inherit** to children; others (margin, border) do not.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** `#nav a` = (1,0,1); `.btn` = (0,1,0). Compare ids first: 1 > 0, so `#nav a` wins.

**Example 2.** `ul li.active` vs `.menu .active`. Step 1: first = (0,1,2). Step 2: second = (0,2,0). Step 3: compare classes: 2 > 1, so `.menu .active` wins even though it has fewer type selectors.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Fighting specificity with `!important` everywhere — it creates an unmaintainable arms race.
- Styling with ids; prefer classes.
- Thinking 11 classes beat 1 id — they never do; columns are compared left to right, not added.

activity.prompt: Match each selector to its specificity.

quiz.why: .a .b p has two class selectors and one type selector, so its specificity is (0,2,1).

quiz.q: Two rules with equal specificity: which wins?
quiz.why: When specificity is equal, the rule that comes later in the CSS wins.
Text properties such as color inherit by default. Margin, padding and border do not.

options: Only li that are direct children of ul
quiz.why: ul > li uses the child combinator. It selects only li elements that are direct children of ul.

quiz.q: Can 20 class selectors beat one id selector?
quiz.why: Specificity is compared column by column and does not carry over. A single id outranks any number of classes.

story.title: The card that would not fit

scenes.text: Arjun sets width: 300px on a card with padding 20px and border 5px. It overflows its 300px slot.
He learns the real width is 350px — until he switches to box-sizing: border-box.

steps.title: Content, padding, border, margin
steps.body:
Every element is a box: **content** → **padding** (inside, takes background) → **border** → **margin** (outside, transparent).

- `box-sizing: content-box` (default): width = content only.
- `box-sizing: border-box`: width includes padding and border.
- Vertical margins of adjacent blocks can **collapse** to the larger one.

steps.title: Units and display
steps.body:
- Absolute: `px`. Relative: `%` (of parent), `em` (of element's font size), `rem` (of root font size), `vw`/`vh` (viewport).
- `display: block` takes full width; `inline` flows in text and ignores width/height; `inline-block` flows but accepts size; `none` removes it.
- `position`: static, relative, absolute (to nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (to viewport), sticky.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** width 300px, padding 20px, border 5px, margin 10px, content-box. Rendered width = 300 + 2×20 + 2×5 = **350px**; space occupied = 350 + 2×10 = **370px**.

**Example 2.** Same with border-box: rendered width = **300px**; content width = 300 − 40 − 10 = **250px**.

**Example 3.** Root font 16px; `1.5rem` = 24px. Inside an element with font-size 20px, `2em` = 40px.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting padding/border add to width in content-box.
- Setting width on inline elements (ignored).
- Using `position: absolute` without a positioned ancestor — it positions against the page.
- Expecting horizontal margins to collapse (only vertical block margins do).

activity.prompt: content-box: width 200px, padding 15px, border 2px. What is the rendered width (excluding margin)?

quiz.q: Which layer takes the element's background colour?
quiz.why: The background is painted under the content and padding (and border). It does not extend into the margin.

quiz.q: With border-box, width 100px, padding 10px: content width?
quiz.why: With border-box, the width includes padding and border. 100px width minus 10px padding on each side leaves 80px for the content.
rem is relative to the root (html) element's font size.

quiz.q: Two stacked blocks, margins 20px and 30px. Gap between them?
quiz.why: Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger one. The gap is 30px, not 50px.
An absolutely positioned element is placed relative to its nearest positioned ancestor, or the initial containing block if there is none.

scenes.text: Priya wants a navbar with the logo left and links right — Flexbox does it in three lines.
Then a photo gallery that is 3 columns on laptops: Grid makes rows and columns together.

steps.title: Flexbox: one dimension
steps.body:
`display: flex` on the container. Main axis set by `flex-direction` (row/column).

- `justify-content` aligns along the main axis (flex-start, center, space-between…).
- `align-items` aligns on the cross axis.
- `flex-wrap: wrap` lets items wrap; `gap` spaces them.
- On items: `flex: 1` (grow), `flex: 0 0 200px` (fixed basis), `order`.

steps.title: Grid: two dimensions
steps.body:
`display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 16px;`

- `fr` = fraction of free space.
- `repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr))` gives a responsive gallery without media queries.
- Items can span: `grid-column: 1 / 3` or `span 2`; named areas with `grid-template-areas`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Navbar.** Step 1: `nav { display:flex; }`. Step 2: `justify-content: space-between;` pushes logo and link group apart. Step 3: `align-items: center;` centres vertically.

**Example 2. Columns 1fr 2fr in 900px with gap 30px.** Free space = 900 − 30 = 870. 1fr = 870/3 = 290px; 2fr = 580px.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Putting `justify-content` on the item instead of the container.
- Expecting `align-items` to work along the main axis.
- Forgetting that `gap` is subtracted before `fr` is computed.
- Using Flexbox for a strict 2-D grid, which leads to uneven columns.

activity.prompt: Write CSS for .gallery so it is a grid with 3 equal columns and a 10px gap.

quiz.why: Flexbox lays items out along one axis at a time, so it is one-dimensional. Grid handles rows and columns together.
With flex-direction: column, the main axis is vertical. So justify-content aligns items vertically.

quiz.q: 1fr 1fr 2fr in 800px, no gap. Width of the last column?
quiz.why: 1fr 1fr 2fr is 4 equal parts. 800px / 4 = 200px per part, so the last column is 2 × 200 = 400px.

quiz.q: Which makes a responsive card grid without media queries?
quiz.why: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)) adds as many columns as fit, so the grid adapts without media queries.
grid-column: 1 / 3 runs from grid line 1 to grid line 3, which covers 2 column tracks.

scenes.text: Dev's shop site looks perfect on his laptop, but his grandfather's phone shows tiny text and sideways scrolling.
He rewrites it mobile-first with fluid images and two breakpoints.

steps.title: Mobile-first media queries
steps.body:
Write base styles for small screens, then add enhancements:

`@media (min-width: 768px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; } }`

- Breakpoints should follow your content, not specific devices.
- Other features: `orientation`, `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion`.

steps.title: Fluid media and typography
steps.body:
- `img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }` prevents overflow.
- `srcset` and `sizes` let the browser choose a smaller image file on phones.
- `clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem)` gives a font size that scales but stays within limits.
- Touch targets of at least about 44×44 CSS px are easier to tap.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Styles: base 1 column; `min-width:600px` → 2 columns; `min-width:1000px` → 4 columns. At 800px: base applies, 600 rule applies, 1000 rule does not → **2 columns**.

**Example 2.** `font-size: clamp(16px, 4vw, 24px)` on a 300px phone: 4vw = 12px < 16 → **16px**. On 1200px: 48px > 24 → **24px**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Desktop-first overrides that pile up and conflict.
- Fixed pixel widths on containers.
- Hiding important content on mobile instead of reorganising it.
- Ignoring `prefers-reduced-motion` for heavy animations.

activity.label: Viewport width for a page with breakpoints at 600px and 1000px

bands.text: Both rules active; the later 1000px rule wins: 4 columns.

quiz.why: Mobile-first CSS starts with the small-screen styles and uses min-width queries to add layout as the screen widens.
max-width: 100% keeps an image within its container, and height: auto keeps its proportions.
3vw of a 1000px viewport is 30px, which is above the maximum 20px. clamp() caps the value at 20px.

quiz.q: Breakpoints should ideally be chosen by…
quiz.why: Choose breakpoints where the content's layout actually breaks, not for specific devices. That lasts longer.

quiz.q: Which media feature respects users who get motion sickness?
quiz.why: prefers-reduced-motion lets CSS reduce or remove animation for users who are sensitive to motion.

questions.q: Specificity of #a .b c?
questions.why: #a .b c has one id, one class and one type selector, so its specificity is (1,1,1).

questions.q: Which wins: inline style or #id selector (no !important)?
questions.why: An inline style has higher priority than any selector, including an id selector, unless !important is used.

questions.q: content-box: width 250, padding 10, border 1. Rendered width?
questions.why: With content-box, the width of 250 is just the content. Padding 10 + 10 and border 1 + 1 add 22, so the rendered width is 272.

questions.q: border-box: width 250, padding 10, border 1. Content width?
questions.why: With border-box, the 250 includes padding and border: 250 − 20 − 2 = 228px for the content.

questions.q: Which display value ignores width and height?
questions.why: Inline elements size by their content and ignore width and height. inline-block, block and flex respect them.

questions.q: justify-content in a row flex container aligns items…
questions.why: In a row flex container, the main axis is horizontal, so justify-content aligns items horizontally.

questions.q: Grid 1fr 3fr in 1000px with gap 40px. First column width?
questions.why: Free space is 1000 − 40 = 960px. Split 1:3, the first column is 960/4 = 240px.

questions.q: The ::before pseudo-element adds…
options: Generated content before the element's content
questions.why: ::before inserts generated content (set with the content property) before the element's own content. It is not in the HTML.

questions.q: Assertion: Vertical margins of adjacent blocks can collapse. Reason: Padding also collapses.
questions.why: Vertical margins of adjacent blocks can collapse, so A is true. Padding never collapses, so R is false.

questions.q: Root 16px, parent font 20px, child 1.5em. Child font size?
questions.why: em is relative to the parent's computed font size. 1.5 × 20px = 30px, not based on the root's 16px.

questions.q: position: sticky behaves like…
options: relative until a scroll threshold, then fixed within its container
questions.why: position: sticky acts like relative until the scroll position passes a threshold, then sticks like fixed within its container.

questions.q: Case: breakpoints at min-width 640 and 1024. At 1024px exactly, which apply?
questions.why: min-width is inclusive. At exactly 1024px, both the 640 and 1024 queries match, plus the base styles.

questions.q: Best tool for a page layout with header, sidebar, content and footer regions?
questions.why: CSS Grid with template areas suits page regions like header, sidebar, content and footer, as they need rows and columns.

questions.q: .nav .item and ul li a: which is more specific?
questions.why: .nav .item has two classes, (0,2,0). ul li a has three type selectors, (0,0,3). A class column outranks any number of type selectors.

questions.q: Which unit is best for accessible, user-scalable font sizes?
questions.why: rem scales from the user's base font size setting, so text respects user preferences. px is fixed.

questions.q: Case: flex items overflow a narrow container on one line. Simplest fix?
questions.why: Setting flex-wrap: wrap lets items move onto new lines when they do not fit, instead of overflowing.

questions.q: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px,1fr)) in a 1100px container with no gap gives how many columns?
questions.why: 250px columns fit floor(1100/250) = 4 times. With auto-fit the 4 columns then stretch to share the space.

courses.title: Unit 3 · JavaScript Core and the DOM
courses.summary: Values and types, scope and closures, arrays and objects with higher-order functions, and manipulating the DOM with events.
outcomes: Learners can explain let/const/var, hoisting and type coercion
Learners can write closures and higher-order functions
Learners can use map, filter and reduce on arrays of objects
Learners can select DOM elements and respond to events with delegation

scenes.text: Sana's bill calculator adds a quantity from an input box and shows 53 instead of 8.
Input values are strings; she converts with Number() and the bug disappears.

steps.title: Primitive types and objects
steps.body:
Primitives: `number`, `string`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `bigint`, `symbol`. Everything else (arrays, functions, dates) is an **object**, passed by reference.

`typeof null` is 'object' — a historic quirk. Use `Array.isArray(x)` for arrays.

steps.title: let, const, var and hoisting
steps.body:
- `const` cannot be reassigned (but a const object's contents can change).
- `let` is block-scoped and reassignable.
- `var` is function-scoped and hoisted with value undefined.
- let/const are hoisted too but sit in the **temporal dead zone** until declared — accessing early throws ReferenceError.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** `'5' + 3` → '53' (+ with a string concatenates). `'5' - 3` → 2 (− converts to number). `'5' * '2'` → 10.

**Example 2.** `0 == ''` is true (both become 0) but `0 === ''` is false (different types). Rule: use `===`.

**Example 3.** Falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. So `if ('0')` runs — a non-empty string is truthy.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using `==` and getting surprising coercion.
- `NaN === NaN` is false; test with `Number.isNaN`.
- Floating point: `0.1 + 0.2` is 0.30000000000000004; round for display or work in paise/cents.
- Mutating a const array and thinking const prevented it.

activity.prompt: The values a and b come from input boxes as strings. Print their numeric sum.
activity.hint: Convert with Number() or parseInt before adding.

quiz.why: typeof null is 'object'. This is a historic quirk of JavaScript.
The minus operator converts both strings to numbers, so '10' − '4' = 6. (+ would concatenate.)
'0' is a non-empty string, so it is truthy. '', null and 0 are falsy.

quiz.q: Accessing a let variable before its declaration…
quiz.why: A let variable is in the temporal dead zone before its declaration. Reading it throws a ReferenceError.
const stops the variable being reassigned, but the array's contents can change. So push works and arr is [1, 2].

scenes.text: Imran needs a like-counter per post without global variables.
A function returning another function carries its own 'backpack' of variables — a closure.

steps.title: Ways to write functions
steps.body:
- Declaration: `function add(a, b) { return a + b; }` (hoisted).
- Expression: `const add = function (a, b) {...}`.
- Arrow: `const add = (a, b) => a + b;` — no own `this`, no `arguments`.
- Default and rest parameters: `function f(x = 1, ...rest)`.

steps.title: Lexical scope and closures
steps.body:
A function can use variables from where it was **defined**. When an inner function outlives its outer function, it keeps access to those variables — that is a **closure**.

Uses: private state, function factories, event handlers, memoisation.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Counter.**
`function makeCounter(){ let n = 0; return () => ++n; }`
`const c = makeCounter(); c(); c();` → returns 1 then 2. A second `makeCounter()` starts its own n at 0.

**Example 2. Loop trap.** `for (var i=0;i<3;i++) setTimeout(()=>console.log(i))` prints 3,3,3 because one shared `i`. With `let`, each iteration gets a new binding → 0,1,2.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using arrow functions as object methods that need `this`.
- Forgetting `return` in a function with braces: `x => { x * 2 }` returns undefined.
- `var` in loops with async callbacks.
- Accidentally creating globals by assigning without declaring.

activity.prompt: Write makeCounter() returning a function that increments and returns a private count. The program should print 1 2 3.
activity.hint: Keep n in the outer function and return an arrow that does ++n.

options: A function plus the variables of the scope it was created in
quiz.why: A closure is a function together with the variables of the scope where it was created. It keeps access to them later.
In x => { x * 2 }, the braces make a function body, so with no return it gives undefined. Without braces, x => x * 2 would return 8.
let creates a new binding of i for each loop iteration, so each callback sees its own i: 0, 1, 2.

quiz.q: Arrow functions do NOT have their own…
quiz.why: Arrow functions have no own this. They use the this of the surrounding scope.

quiz.q: Which is hoisted with its body?
quiz.why: Function declarations are fully hoisted, including their body. Function expressions in let or const are not usable before their line.

scenes.text: Prof. Iyer has an array of 60 student objects and needs pass list, average and toppers.
Instead of three for-loops, filter, map and reduce do it in readable chains.

steps.title: Objects and destructuring
steps.body:
Object: `const s = {name: 'Ana', marks: 82};` Access `s.name` or `s['name']`.

- Destructuring: `const {name, marks} = s;` and `const [first, ...rest] = arr;`
- Spread copies: `{...s, marks: 90}`, `[...arr, 4]` (shallow copies).
- `Object.keys`, `Object.values`, `Object.entries`; JSON.stringify/parse.

steps.title: map, filter, reduce, find, some, every
steps.body:
- `map(fn)` → new array, same length, transformed.
- `filter(fn)` → new array of items where fn is true.
- `reduce((acc, x) => ..., init)` → one value.
- `find` → first match or undefined; `some`/`every` → boolean.
- `sort` mutates; for numbers pass `(a, b) => a - b`.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** marks = [45, 82, 30, 91]. Passed (≥40): `marks.filter(m => m >= 40)` → [45, 82, 91].

**Example 2.** Average: `marks.reduce((a, m) => a + m, 0) / marks.length` → 248/4 = **62**.

**Example 3.** `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives [1, 10, 9] because default sort compares strings. `sort((a,b)=>a-b)` gives [1, 9, 10].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting the initial value in reduce (empty arrays then throw).
- Expecting `map` to filter out items.
- Default `sort()` on numbers.
- Thinking spread makes a deep copy — nested objects are still shared.

activity.prompt: Print the names of students with marks of at least 40, joined by commas.
activity.hint: filter, then map to names, then join(',').

quiz.why: map applies the function to every item and returns a new array: [2, 4, 6].
sort() compares as strings by default. '10' sorts before '5', giving [1, 10, 5]. Pass a compare function to sort numbers.
reduce adds 2 + 4 + 6 starting from 0, which is 12.
find returns undefined if nothing matches. findIndex returns −1.

quiz.q: const b = {...a} where a has a nested object. Changing b.inner.x…
quiz.why: Spread copies only the top level (a shallow copy). Nested objects are shared, so changing b.inner.x also changes a.inner.x.

story.title: The to-do list that forgot new items

scenes.text: Lata attaches a click handler to every delete button, but buttons added later do nothing.
She uses event delegation: one listener on the list catches clicks from any current or future button.

steps.title: Selecting and changing elements
steps.body:
- `document.querySelector('.card')`, `querySelectorAll('li')` (static NodeList), `getElementById('x')`.
- Change text: `el.textContent = 'Hi'`. Classes: `el.classList.add/remove/toggle('done')`. Attributes: `el.setAttribute`, `el.dataset.id`.
- Create: `const li = document.createElement('li'); list.append(li);` Remove: `li.remove()`.

steps.title: Events, bubbling and delegation
steps.body:
`btn.addEventListener('click', handler)`. The handler gets an **event** object: `e.target` (what was clicked), `e.currentTarget` (where the listener is), `e.preventDefault()` (e.g. stop form reload), `e.stopPropagation()`.

Events **bubble** up from the target to ancestors, so a parent can handle children's events — **delegation**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1. Delegated delete.**
`list.addEventListener('click', e => { if (e.target.matches('button.del')) e.target.closest('li').remove(); });`
Step 1: one listener. Step 2: check what was clicked. Step 3: remove its li.

**Example 2. Form submit without reload.** `form.addEventListener('submit', e => { e.preventDefault(); ... })`.

steps.title: Common mistakes (including a security one)
steps.body:
- Using `innerHTML` with user-typed text: it interprets markup and can let attacker-controlled content run in your page (cross-site scripting). Use `textContent` for user data.
- Running scripts before the DOM exists — use `defer` on the script tag.
- Adding listeners inside loops instead of delegating.
- Confusing `e.target` with `e.currentTarget`.

activity.prompt: Event bubbling simulation: given the path of elements an event bubbles through, print them joined by ' > ' starting from the target.
activity.starter:
const path = ['button', 'li', 'ul', 'body'];
// print: button > li > ul > body
activity.hint: Bubbling goes from the target upward; join the array.

quiz.q: Safest way to show a user's comment text?
quiz.why: textContent inserts text without parsing it as HTML, so scripts cannot run. innerHTML parses markup and can allow XSS.
Event delegation relies on bubbling: an event on a child rises to ancestors, so one handler on the parent can handle many children.
preventDefault() cancels the default action. On a form submit, it stops the page from submitting and reloading.
querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList of the matching elements. It does not update when the DOM changes.

quiz.q: The defer attribute makes a script…
options: Run after HTML is parsed, in order
quiz.why: A script with defer downloads while the HTML parses and runs after parsing is done, in the order of the tags.

questions.q: typeof [] is…
questions.why: typeof [] is 'object', since arrays are objects. Use Array.isArray to test for an array.
The * operator converts both strings to numbers, so '3' * '4' = 12 (a number).

questions.q: null == undefined and null === undefined are…
questions.why: null == undefined is true (loose equality), but null === undefined is false since they are different types.

questions.q: Which keyword is function-scoped?
questions.why: var is function-scoped, whereas let and const are block-scoped.

questions.q: Output: let x = 1; { let x = 2; } console.log(x)
questions.why: The inner x is block-scoped to its braces. Outside it, x is still 1.

questions.q: makeAdder = a => b => a + b; makeAdder(5)(3) =
questions.why: makeAdder(5) returns a function that remembers a = 5 (a closure). Calling it with 3 gives 5 + 3 = 8.
filter(x => x % 2) keeps the odd numbers 1 and 3. map then multiplies by 10, giving [10, 30].

Without a compare function, sort() converts items to strings and compares them character by character: "100" comes before "20", which comes before "3". So the result is [100, 20, 3]. Use .sort((a, b) => a - b) to sort numbers.
0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in binary floating point. So strict equality with 0.3 is false.

questions.q: Assertion: Arrow functions are good object methods that use this. Reason: Arrows take this from the surrounding scope.
questions.why: Arrow functions take this from the surrounding scope, so R is true. That makes them poor object methods, because this will not be the object. So A is false.

questions.q: Which avoids cross-site scripting when inserting user text?
questions.why: textContent treats the value as plain text, so no markup or scripts run. innerHTML, document.write and eval can execute injected code.

questions.q: In a delegated list click handler, which property identifies the clicked button?
questions.why: In a delegated handler, e.target is the element that was actually clicked, such as the button. currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to, e.g. the list.

questions.q: [].reduce((a,b)=>a+b) (no initial value) …
questions.why: reduce on an empty array with no initial value has nothing to start from, so it throws a TypeError.

questions.q: Case: for (var i=0;i<3;i++){ setTimeout(()=>console.log(i),0) } prints?
questions.why: All callbacks share one var i. By the time they run (after the loop), i is 3, so it prints 3 3 3.

questions.q: const {a, ...rest} = {a:1, b:2, c:3}; rest is…
questions.why: The rest pattern collects the remaining properties into a new object: {b: 2, c: 3}.

questions.q: Number.isNaN('abc') vs isNaN('abc')
questions.why: Global isNaN('abc') converts the string to a number (NaN) and gives true. Number.isNaN('abc') does not convert, and a string is not NaN, so false.

courses.title: Unit 4 · Asynchronous JavaScript, HTTP and Web APIs
courses.summary: The event loop, callbacks, promises and async/await; HTTP methods, status codes and REST; fetch, JSON, browser storage and web security basics.
outcomes: Learners can predict output order using the event loop (microtasks vs macrotasks)
Learners can write promise chains and async/await with error handling
Learners can explain HTTP methods, status codes and REST conventions
Learners can choose between cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage safely

scenes.text: Rohan writes setTimeout(..., 0) expecting it to run immediately, but 'done' prints before it.
He draws the call stack, the task queue and the microtask queue — and the order finally makes sense.

steps.title: One thread, many waiting jobs
steps.body:
JavaScript runs on a single main thread with a **call stack**. Slow work (timers, network) is handled by the browser/Node, and callbacks are queued.

- **Macrotask (task) queue**: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events.
- **Microtask queue**: promise callbacks (`then`, `await` continuations), `queueMicrotask`.
- Loop: run the current script → empty **all** microtasks → take **one** task → repeat.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.**
`console.log('A'); setTimeout(()=>console.log('B'),0); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log('C')); console.log('D');`
Step 1: sync logs A, D. Step 2: microtasks: C. Step 3: task: B. Output **A D C B**.

**Example 2.** A loop of 2 seconds of heavy computation blocks clicks and rendering for 2 seconds, because the stack never empties. Fix: split work, or use a Web Worker.

steps.title: setTimeout(fn, 0) means 'at least 0 ms'
steps.body: It means 'queue as a task after at least this delay', not 'run now'. Browsers may clamp nested timers to about 4 ms.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking async code runs in parallel threads on the main thread.
- Blocking the main thread with long synchronous loops.
- Expecting setTimeout delays to be exact.

activity.prompt: Predict, then run: make the program print the letters in the order they actually appear, separated by spaces, on one line. (Collect them in an array and print at the end with a timeout.)
activity.hint: Sync first, then microtasks, then timers.

quiz.why: Promise .then callbacks are queued as microtasks. They run before the next task such as a timer.

quiz.q: After each task the event loop…
quiz.why: After each task, the event loop runs all queued microtasks until the microtask queue is empty.

quiz.q: Output of: log 1; setTimeout(log 2); then(log 3); log 4
quiz.why: Synchronous logs run first (1, 4). Then the promise callback (a microtask) logs 3. The setTimeout callback is a later task, so 2 is last: 1 4 3 2.
JavaScript on the main thread cannot render or respond while a long synchronous loop runs. The page freezes.

quiz.q: Heavy computation without freezing the UI can use…
quiz.why: Web Workers run scripts on a separate thread, so heavy computation does not block the UI.

scenes.text: Kavya's code loads a user, then orders, then invoices — five nested callbacks deep.
Rewritten with async/await and try/catch, it reads top to bottom like normal code.

steps.title: Promise states
steps.body:
A Promise is **pending**, then settles once as **fulfilled** (with a value) or **rejected** (with a reason).

- `.then(onOk)` returns a new promise → chaining.
- `.catch(onErr)` handles any earlier rejection; `.finally` runs either way.
- Combinators: `Promise.all` (all must succeed, fails fast), `Promise.allSettled` (all results), `Promise.race`, `Promise.any`.

steps.title: async/await
steps.body:
An `async` function always returns a promise. `await p` pauses that function (not the thread) until p settles.

Use `try { await ... } catch (e) { ... }` for errors. Independent requests should run in parallel: `const [a, b] = await Promise.all([getA(), getB()]);`

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Two independent 1-second requests: awaiting one after the other takes ~2 s; `Promise.all` takes ~1 s.

**Example 2.** `Promise.all([ok(1), fail('x'), ok(3)])` rejects with 'x' as soon as fail rejects; `allSettled` gives [{status:'fulfilled',value:1},{status:'rejected',reason:'x'},{status:'fulfilled',value:3}].

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Forgetting `return` inside `.then`, breaking the chain.
- Using `await` inside `forEach` (it doesn't wait); use `for...of` or `Promise.all`.
- Unhandled rejections because there is no catch.
- Awaiting independent tasks sequentially.

activity.prompt: Use Promise.all to wait for both fake requests, then print the sum of their results (should print 30).
activity.hint: Destructure the array returned by Promise.all.

quiz.why: An async function always returns a promise. A returned value is wrapped in a resolved promise.
Promise.all rejects as soon as any one of the promises rejects (fail-fast).

quiz.q: To get every outcome regardless of failure use…
quiz.why: Promise.allSettled waits for all promises and reports each result, whether fulfilled or rejected.
forEach ignores the promises returned by its callback. So awaiting inside it does not make the outer code wait.

quiz.q: A promise can settle how many times?
quiz.why: A promise settles once, to fulfilled or rejected. Its state then cannot change.

scenes.text: Tanvi's weather widget says 'city not found' — but the server actually replied 401 because her token expired.
She learns to read status codes and check response.ok before using data.

steps.title: Request and response
steps.body:
A request has a **method**, URL, headers and optional body. A response has a **status code**, headers and body.

- GET read · POST create · PUT replace · PATCH partial update · DELETE remove.
- **Safe** methods (GET, HEAD) don't change state; **idempotent** ones (GET, PUT, DELETE) give the same result if repeated; POST is neither.
- Status classes: 1xx info, 2xx success (200, 201, 204), 3xx redirect (301, 304), 4xx client error (400, 401, 403, 404, 429), 5xx server error (500, 503).

steps.title: REST conventions and fetch
steps.body:
Resources are nouns: `GET /students`, `GET /students/42`, `POST /students`, `PATCH /students/42`, `DELETE /students/42`.

`const res = await fetch(url, {method:'POST', headers:{'Content-Type':'application/json'}, body: JSON.stringify(data)});`
`fetch` only rejects on network failure — a 404 still resolves, so check `res.ok` (true for 200–299).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1.** Pick the status: created a new record → **201**; deleted with no body → **204**; not logged in → **401**; logged in but not allowed → **403**; too many requests → **429**.

**Example 2. CORS.** A page on site A calls an API on site B. The browser blocks reading the response unless B sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` permitting A. CORS is enforced by browsers to protect users; it is configured on the server.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Assuming fetch throws on 4xx/5xx.
- Forgetting `Content-Type: application/json` and JSON.stringify.
- Verbs in REST paths like `/getStudents`.
- Confusing 401 (unauthenticated) and 403 (forbidden).

activity.prompt: Match the situation to the HTTP status code.

quiz.why: PUT is idempotent: repeating the same request leaves the same state. POST can create a new resource each time.
fetch rejects only on network failure. HTTP error statuses like 404 or 500 still resolve, so check res.ok.
res.ok is true for status codes 200 to 299.

quiz.q: RESTful path to update student 7 partially?
quiz.why: A REST update uses a noun path and an HTTP method. PATCH /students/7 partially updates student 7.
CORS is enforced by the browser, which decides whether a web page may read a cross-origin response.

lessons.title: JSON, storage and web security basics

scenes.text: A tutorial told Yash to store his login token in localStorage.
His mentor explains why an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie reduces the damage if any script is injected.

steps.title: JSON
steps.body:
JSON is text: objects `{}`, arrays `[]`, strings in double quotes, numbers, true/false/null. No functions, comments, undefined or trailing commas.

`JSON.stringify(obj)` → text; `JSON.parse(text)` → value (throws on invalid JSON, so wrap in try/catch).

steps.title: Storage options
steps.body:
- **localStorage**: ~5 MB per origin, persists, strings only, readable by any script on the page.
- **sessionStorage**: same but per tab, cleared when tab closes.
- **Cookies**: small, sent with requests; flags `HttpOnly` (hidden from JS), `Secure` (HTTPS only), `SameSite` (limits cross-site sending).
- **IndexedDB**: larger structured client storage.

steps.title: Defensive basics every web developer needs
steps.body:
- Always use **HTTPS**.
- Treat all input as untrusted: validate on the server, encode output (textContent), use parameterised database queries.
- Add a **Content-Security-Policy** header to restrict where scripts may load from.
- Protect state-changing requests from cross-site request forgery with SameSite cookies and anti-CSRF tokens.
- Never put secrets (API keys) in front-end code — anyone can read it.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Storing objects in localStorage without JSON.stringify (you get '[object Object]').
- Storing passwords or long-lived tokens in localStorage.
- Trusting data from localStorage as if it were validated.
- Shipping API secrets inside the JavaScript bundle.

activity.prompt: Convert the object to JSON text and back, then print the parsed name.

quiz.why: Valid JSON needs double-quoted keys and strings, no functions and no trailing commas. {"name":"a"} is valid.

quiz.q: Which cookie flag hides it from JavaScript?
quiz.why: The HttpOnly flag hides a cookie from JavaScript, so a script injected by XSS cannot read it.
sessionStorage lives for the tab session, so it is cleared when the tab closes. localStorage persists.

quiz.q: Where should a private API key live?
quiz.why: Front-end code is visible to every user. Private API keys must stay on the server.
Web storage holds only strings. An object is converted with toString, giving '[object Object]'. Use JSON.stringify first.

questions.q: JavaScript in the browser runs user code on…
questions.why: The browser runs your JavaScript on a single main thread, using an event loop.

questions.q: Which runs first after synchronous code finishes?
questions.why: After synchronous code ends, microtasks like Promise.then callbacks run before timer callbacks.

questions.q: Output: setTimeout(()=>log('t')); queueMicrotask(()=>log('m')); log('s')
questions.why: The synchronous log s runs first. The microtask m runs next, and the timer task t runs last: s m t.

questions.q: Status for 'logged in but lacking permission'?
questions.why: 403 Forbidden means you are logged in but not permitted. 401 means not authenticated.

questions.q: Which method is neither safe nor idempotent?
questions.why: POST is not safe (it changes state) and not idempotent (repeating can create duplicates). GET is safe, and PUT and DELETE are idempotent.

questions.q: fetch('/missing') returns 404. The promise…
questions.why: fetch resolves even for a 404, with res.ok false. It rejects only on network failure.

questions.q: Three independent 500 ms requests awaited one after another take about…
questions.why: Awaiting each request in turn means they run one after another: 3 × 500 = 1500 ms.

questions.q: Same three with Promise.all take about…
questions.why: Promise.all starts the three requests together, so they overlap. The total time is about the longest one, 500 ms.

questions.q: Promise.any resolves when…
questions.why: Promise.any resolves with the first promise that succeeds. It ignores rejections unless all of them fail.

questions.q: Assertion: CORS protects servers from all attacks. Reason: CORS is enforced by browsers.
questions.why: CORS is enforced by browsers, so R is true. But it controls what a web page may read, and it does not protect a server from attacks, so A is false.

questions.q: JSON.parse("{'a':1}") …
questions.why: JSON requires double quotes. {'a':1} with single quotes is invalid, so JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError.

questions.q: Best cookie settings for a session id?
questions.why: HttpOnly hides the cookie from scripts, Secure sends it only over HTTPS, and SameSite limits cross-site sending. Together they reduce theft and misuse of a session id.

questions.q: A Content-Security-Policy header mainly…
options: Restricts which sources scripts and resources may load from
questions.why: A Content-Security-Policy tells the browser which sources it may load scripts and other resources from. It limits the damage from injected scripts.

questions.q: Case: an async function uses await inside arr.forEach and logs 'done' after. 'done' prints…
questions.why: forEach does not wait for async callbacks. So the line after it runs, printing done, before the awaited work finishes.

questions.q: HTTP 304 means…
options: Not modified — use the cached copy
questions.why: HTTP 304 means Not Modified: the client's cached copy is still valid and can be used.

questions.q: Which REST design is best for listing a student's courses?
questions.why: A REST design uses nouns and nesting, with the method giving the action. GET /students/4/courses lists student 4's courses.

quiz.q: Which is the cross-axis alignment property in Flexbox?
quiz.why: align-items sets alignment along the cross axis in Flexbox. justify-content works on the main axis.
An empty alt (alt="") marks an image as purely decorative. Screen readers then skip it instead of reading out a file name.
Count by specificity. .a .b .c has three classes (0,3,0), while .a.b has two (0,2,0). The higher specificity wins.

scenes.text: The examiner asks: 'Explain the event loop in one minute.'
You answer: stack, then all microtasks, then one task — and give an example.

steps.title: JavaScript essentials
steps.body:
- Use const by default, let when reassigning, avoid var.
- Use === ; falsy: false, 0, '', null, undefined, NaN.
- Closures remember their defining scope.
- map/filter/reduce return new values; sort mutates and needs (a,b)=>a-b for numbers.
- Use textContent for user text.

steps.title: Async and HTTP essentials
steps.body:
- Order: sync → microtasks (promises) → one task (timers).
- async returns a promise; use try/catch; Promise.all for parallel.
- fetch resolves on 404/500 — check res.ok.
- 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 301, 304, 400, 401, 403, 404, 429, 500, 503.
- Cookies for sessions: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite.

PUT is idempotent.
statements.why: Repeated PUT yields the same state.

statements.s: localStorage is a safe place for secrets.
statements.why: Any page script can read it.

quiz.q: Which CSS layout suits a one-row toolbar?
quiz.why: A one-row toolbar needs layout along one axis, which is exactly what Flexbox is for. Grid is for two-dimensional layouts.

quiz.q: Which JS method returns a boolean if any element matches?
quiz.why: some returns true if at least one element satisfies the test. find returns the element, and filter returns an array.

quiz.q: Which HTML attribute makes a field mandatory?
quiz.why: The required attribute makes a form field mandatory before submission.

questions.q: Which tag holds metadata like charset?
questions.why: <head> holds page metadata such as the charset and title. Visible content goes in <body>.

questions.q: Which selector targets only direct li children of .menu?
questions.why: .menu > li uses the child combinator, selecting only li elements that are direct children of .menu.

questions.q: content-box width 300, padding 12, border 3, margin 5. Horizontal space occupied?
questions.why: With content-box, the space used is width + padding + border + margin = 300 + 2·12 + 2·3 + 2·5 = 300 + 24 + 6 + 10 = 340.

questions.q: Grid 2fr 1fr 1fr in 1240px with two 20px gaps. First column?
questions.why: Free space is 1240 − 2·20 = 1200px. Split in 4 parts, one part is 300px, so the first column (2fr) is 600px.
+ with a string joins: '2' + 2 = '22'. Then − converts to numbers: 22 − 1 = 21.
The compare function b − a sorts in descending order, giving [10, 5, 1].

questions.q: Which correctly runs two awaits in parallel?
questions.why: await Promise.all([a(), b()]) starts both and waits for both together, so they run in parallel. Two separate awaits run one after the other.

questions.q: Status for a successful DELETE with no body?
questions.why: 204 No Content is the usual status for a successful DELETE that returns no body.

questions.q: Which is NOT falsy?
questions.why: Empty string, 0 and NaN are falsy. An empty array [] is an object, so it is truthy.

questions.q: Event that bubbles from a button reaches which first?
questions.why: Events bubble upward one level at a time. From a button, the first to receive it is its parent element.

questions.q: Case: a page shows comments using innerHTML. What change best reduces injected-script risk?
questions.why: innerHTML parses user text as markup, which can run injected scripts. Use textContent to treat it as plain text, and add a Content Security Policy as another layer.

questions.q: Which statement about const is correct?
questions.why: const prevents reassigning the variable, but the contents of an object or array it holds can still change.

questions.q: Assertion: min-width media queries suit mobile-first CSS. Reason: Styles are added as the viewport gets wider.
options: Both true, R doesn't explain A
questions.why: Mobile-first CSS starts with small-screen styles and adds more as the viewport widens, which is what min-width queries do. So the reason explains the assertion.

questions.q: Output: let a=[1,2]; let b=a; b.push(3); console.log(a.length)
questions.why: b = a copies the reference, so both names refer to the same array. After b.push(3), a.length is 3.

questions.q: Which HTTP header must the API send to allow a different origin to read the response?
questions.why: The server must send the Access-Control-Allow-Origin header to let a page from another origin read its response (CORS).

questions.q: Output order: log A; setTimeout(log B); Promise.resolve().then(()=>{log C; setTimeout(log D)}); log E
questions.why: Synchronous logs run first: A, E. Then the promise microtask logs C and schedules timer D. The earlier timer B runs before D, so A E C B D.

questions.q: Accessible name for <input id='q'> is best given by…
questions.why: A <label for="q"> gives the input a visible, accessible name. A placeholder or title alone is a weaker substitute.

questions.q: clamp(12px, 5vw, 28px) on a 400px screen =
questions.why: 5vw of a 400px screen is 20px. That is between 12px and 28px, so clamp gives 20px.
